subsubtopic: PRESENTATION OF FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present the first report of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts. Pursuant to Standing Order 99(2) the committee requests a comprehensive response.
This report deals with the income tax remission order granted to Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company, a subsidiary of Dome Petroleum Limited. The committee is concerned that the remission order conferred a substantial benefit without Parliament's approval. The remission was used in an unconventional and unprecedented way to implement government policy rather than to provide relief from an aspect of the tax system. Moreover, the amount of the remission was not disclosed in the public accounts as required under the Financial Administration Act. The use of a remission order in this way denied Parliament an opportunity to consider a significant expenditure of public funds.
The committee is recommending that disclosure of all income tax remission orders be required and, further, that prior parliamentary approval be required for remissions exceeding $20 million in value.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE AND CANADA EVIDENCE ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-15, an Act to amend the Criminal Code and the Canada Evidence Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is an honour today to address the House on a matter of grave concern for all Canadians-child sexual abuse. We are here to do something about this. Our younger generation is the promise of Canada's future. We have a responsibility to protect children from sexual abuse and exploitation and to deter those who would seek to victimize them.
It is a high priority of the Government and myself, as Minister of Justice, to address this issue in an effective and sensitive manner. To that end I am asking for the support of all Members in this House in order that this legislation may be dealt with without delay so that those children who are
November 4, 1986

presently being exploited can have some protection under the law.
In 1984, the Committee on Sexual Offences against Children and Youths, the Badgely Committee, reported that half of all Canadian females and one-third of males are at some time victims of unwanted sexual acts, 80 per cent of which occur when the victims are children or youths. Over the last two years police departments and child welfare agencies have seen a significant increase in the rate of reporting of child sexual abuse cases by as much as 25 per cent to 50 per cent.

This disturbing increase in the number of cases reported is in some measure due to the fact that both the experts and the general public are now more aware of the problem of sexual offences against children. Furthermore, children themselves are also better aware of the parameters of this problem, thanks to educational programs that teach children not to submit to the various physical advances that may be made by their elders or by persons in a position of authority.

In April, 1985, the report of the Special Committee on Pornography and Prostitution, known as the Fraser Report, was published. The work of the Fraser Committee in part overlapped that of the Badgley Committee so that recommendations were made by both committees on certain aspects of child sexual abuse such as the provisions presently existing in the Criminal Code which are applicable to child sexual abuse and to juvenile prostitution.
The Badgely Committee and the Fraser Committee have made a significant contribution in identifying the scope of the child sexual abuse problems in Canada in those areas where present legal provisions have failed us. In addition, officials in the Department of Justice and other concerned Departments have met with more than 300 individuals representing more than 200 different organizations across Canada to gather the views of certain non governmental organizations and private sector agencies concerned with children's issues about the recommendations of these committees. Consultations were also conducted with the provinces. As a result of the review of the recommendations of the two committees, and these consultations, legislative amendments were developed to deal with the problems of child sexual abuse, reception of children's evidence and juvenile prostitution. The findings of the Badgley and Fraser Committees and the consultations with the provinces and the public clearly pointed out that the present Criminal Code provisions do not adequately cover the full range of sexual behaviour that children may be induced to engage in, nor are young girls and boys afforded the equal degree of protection of the law required by our Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
This Bill would create three new criminal offences, namely sexual interference, invitation to sexual touching, and sexual
Criminal Code
exploitation, to ensure that children under 14 years of age are protected almost absolutely from all manner of sexual contact while children up to the age of 18 years would be protected from sexual exploitation by anyone in a position of trust or authority or on whom the child is dependent.
The new offence of sexual interference is designed to cover a wide range of sexually abusive behaviour consistent with the Badgley recommendations. The consent of the child to being touched for a sexual purpose is irrelevant. The child is to be protected from all touchings for a sexual purpose, with one exception. This exception would cover youths aged 12 or 13 who are not more than three years older than the complainant. Of course, if the complainant under 14 did not consent to the sexual activity with a 12 or 13 year old accused, the young accused could be charged under present sexual assault provisions.
Since the age of criminal responsibility is 12, children under 12 would not be held criminally responsible for any sexual activity. Over-all, the effect of this new offence would be to provide an almost absolute protection to children under 14 years of age from being touched for a sexual purpose.
The Badgley Committee found that very young children were sometimes bribed or otherwise induced to perform sexual acts upon another individual. Under the present law, no sexual assault is committed by the inviter in this situation and prosecution under the indecent act provisions may not always be successful.
In order to ensure more complete protection for children under 14 from all manner of sexual abuse, a new offence would be created termed invitation to sexual touching. It would be an offence for anyone to invite a child under 14 to touch him or her for a sexual purpose. It would also be an offence for anyone to invite young children to engage in sexual touching of themselves or others.
The two new offences which would afford protection to those under 14, sexual interference and invitation to sexual touching, would be hybrid offences with Crown election whether to proceed by way of indictment or summary conviction. Where the Crown decided to proceed by way of indictment, the maximum penalty available would be a ten-year sentence of imprisonment.
The proposed third new offence, that of sexual exploitation, would protect young people under the age of 18 from sexual activity with an adult who is either in a position of trust or authority, or on whom this young person is in a relationship of dependency. This offence recognizes that a young person requires special protection from those individuals who would use their position of authority, or the child's trust or dependency to exploit them.
There was a great deal of concern expressed by child care workers and others, as well as by the Badgley and Fraser Committees that those accused of sexual offences against children should not be able to avoid prosecution easily by arguing they did not know the age of the child involved. With

November 4, 1986
Criminal Code
respect to the three new offences, and in fact all the provisions that would protect children, mistake of age will not be a defence unless the accused took every reasonable step to ascertain the age of the complainant.
There is another form of sexual abuse of our youth that has increasingly been openly practised across Canada. It is the exploitation of our children by those who seek their services as prostitutes and by those who would benefit financially from putting them to work as prostitutes. This Bill would create a new indictable offence punishable by a maximum sentence of five years for anyone in any place to obtain the services of a juvenile prostitute. Both the Badgley and Fraser Committees recommended penalizing the customer of a young prostitute, as did the Standing Committee of the House of Commons on Justice and Legal Affairs in 1983 in its report on prostitution.
The House may recall that I had the honour of being my Party's spokesperson on the Justice and Legal Affairs Committee at the time. I recall the deliberations and many thoughtful presentations made to that committee by individuals and groups across Canada. It is my honour today, as Minister of Justice, to be putting forward legislative changes to deal with the problems addressed by the Justice Committee three years ago. This Bill would also increase the penalties for living from the avails of a prostitute from the present ten-year maximum sentence of imprisonment to 14 years, if a young prostitute under 18 was involved.
[ Translation]
It is not sufficient, however, to create new sexual offences and to amend the present provisions of the Criminal Code accordingly. As the Badgley Committee pointed out and as consultation with non-governmental organizations has confirmed, it often happens that very young children cannot benefit from the protection of criminal law because they cannot be sworn and, consequently, cannot testify in court. Those who abuse very young children can often do so a number of times or abuse more than one child without having much to fear from the law.
The Bill we are about to consider provides a number of amendments to the Criminal Code and the Canada Evidence Act, in order to resolve the problem of the admissibility of evidence given by children and to put in place more flexible mechanisms to gather that evidence.

An amendment to the Criminal Code would remove the current need for corroboration before a conviction can be sustained when it is based only on the unsworn evidence of a child. Amendments to the Canada Evidence Act to enable more children to testify would provide a procedure whereby a judge would examine a child under 14 to determine whether the child could be sworn or heard to affirm. If the child cannot be sworn or make an affirmation, the judge would determine whether the child could be heard on promising to tell the truth. The weight to be given to such evidence would, of course, be a matter for the judge or jury to decide.
A further proposal would abrogate the doctrine of recent complaint. It has been observed that children are frequently unable to bring themselves to make a disclosure of their sexual victimization until a significant time has passed. This inability has resulted in offenders evading prosecution and indeed punishment.
It is also proposed that a videotape of a child victim under 18 describing the acts complained of could be shown in court if the child adopted the contents while testifying. During the series of consultations held with groups and individuals across Canada, my officials were told of numerous instances where young children felt intimidated by the nearness of the accused in the courtroom. Further amendments would permit the judge to exclude the accused from the courtroom during the testimony of the child complainant in a sexual offence case, if the judge believes that the exclusion of the accused is necessary to obtain a full and candid testimony from a child. The excluded accused would, of course, be able to watch the proceedings on closed circuit television and would have the facility and ability to communicate with his or her legal counsel.
We have often heard that sexual abuse is a cyclical problem, that individuals who are abused as children often abuse children in their adult years. It is my hope that this legislation will assist in breaking that cycle of abuse by using our system of justice to protect those who cannot protect themselves, the innocent victims of child sexual abuse. It is not my intention to hold out these amendments to the Criminal Code and the Canada Evidence Act as a solution in and of themselves to the complex and tragic problem of child sexual abuse. However, and this I stress, these amendments are an integral part of the commitment of the federal Government to do everything reasonably possible to stop this damaging conduct.
My colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), is actively co-ordinating an effective federal approach at the policy and program level to combat child sexual abuse. My colleagues and I will be working closely with the provinces and territories to ensure an integrated effort. The amendments before the House, in the context of all the other steps being taken, will send out a real signal that society will not tolerate the continuation of child sexual abuse and exploitation. We will use the full weight of the criminal law to afford our children the protection they have the right to expect.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my Party, her Majesty's Official Opposition, I am very happy to participate in the debate. I begin by assuring the Government and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) that we support action in this area. We welcome the Bill. While we have some concerns I will deal with in a moment, we feel this is an important area for action with respect to Criminal Code amendments. Even before the-
November 4, 1986



Even before the Badgley Report, there was a feeling among the general public about the seriousness of child abuse and people realized that it was a matter that had not been satisfactorily addressed by our society. What really came out of the Badgley Report was that the extent of the problem was far greater than anyone had suspected.

A problem was revealed by the Badgley Commission of a proportion which could hardly have been anticipated by many Canadians. The Badgley Report makes recommendations for many bodies to act on. While there are recommendations which cannot be implemented by Government, there are a certain number which can be, including strengthening the Criminal Code to deal with the problem of child abuse and molestation of children. I am very glad the Government has reintroduced this legislation. I would have been happy to deal with it in the last session of Parliament but I am glad it has been raised in this session. I look forward to the important work the committee will do in looking at the recommendations and to seeing this Bill legislated, hopefully, in this session of Parliament.
Let me say, however, that I think we have to give the public more time to react to the Bill than we seem to be doing. It is true that this Bill is virtually the same as Bill C-114, but 1 do not think too many of the groups which looked at Bill C-114 realize that the Bill has been reintroduced in this session. I hope that, when it comes to committee, at least three or four weeks' notice will be given to communities which are interested, that the Bill is here, that important considerations are before Parliament in this area, that new crimes are being created and that traditional safeguards for the accused are being removed, so that there will be some opportunity for those interested in these questions to get their act together and put a submission in before the parliamentary committee. I think the committee's work will be important because we are creating new crimes and removing traditional safeguards which accused have relied on in the past in connection with offences against young children
I think it important that there be new crimes created and that some of the safeguards which have prevented cases from getting to court in the past be looked at and removed. Nevertheless, when we make changes such as that, it is important they be done with notice and opportunity so that members of the Committee on Justice can consider all the points of view which have to be brought to bear before steps are taken.
A fundamental step on which we must all agree, I submit on behalf of the Official Opposition, is to find ways of getting more cases where young people are sexually abused before the courts of the land. Whatever the safeguards and definitions of the past, the Badgley Report is right in observing that not enough cases have come before the courts. I think judicial decisions, condemnations and judgments against accused in
Criminal Code
connection with sexual offences have an enormous deterrent effect.
People have felt comfortable about getting away with sexual abuse partly because it involved the family where, one might have wrongly felt in the past, the law did not venture and partly because children were involved. Offenders might have felt, because of their more powerful position, that they could get away with it. Whatever the reasons, we have to throw light on this area of behaviour and bring reprehensible behaviour before the courts and obtain more convictions.
There have been barriers in the past which have prevented these cases from coming forward. In part, this has been because of definitions. As the Minister has indicated, and here he has our support, some new offences are being created with new definitions of unacceptable behaviour in relation to young people. I am particularly pleased to see the particular provision with respect to "persons in authority". I am pleased with the provision with respect to the protection of children under 14 and of the greater precision which is attached to the exemption for sex play among children which we must recognize is a normal part of growing up through adolescence. The law must recognize that, and is doing so, with the exception provided for in that provision. But that is not an exception from which an adult should be able to benefit. Again, the Minister's provision makes it clear that exploitation by adults of young children for sexual purposes by adults will be a punishable activity. It will be a crime and will be brought before the courts, if it can be.
On the other side, there is a treatment of the traditional barriers which have prevented behaviour of this type from coming before the courts. There is, first, the qualification of the complainant. The Government is proposing the removal of the requirement that corroboration be retained. If one looks at the cases, one sees that the kind of corroboration asked for by the courts has provided cover and has made it impossible to bring forward many cases which should have been brought forward. Where an adult organizes his assault on the young person with care, corroboration will not be available. Those of us who have practised in the area, and Members of Parliament who have followed the amendments of the Criminal Code in this area in the past, know that the corroboration requirement, which has no counterpart for offences against adults, has probably been the single greatest reason why cases have not been able to be developed to the point where they can be brought before the court. This requirement is to be removed.
Second, we are looking at the acceptability of the complainant's evidence. Is the young person competent to tell a story? Is the young person aware enough of the consequences of what he or she is doing? Is he or she conscious of the difference between truth and falsehood so that a court can be asked to accept such evidence?
We are moving from a point in the law at which courts focused on admissibility to a point where they now focus on questions of weight. In general, I welcome very much this

November 4, 1986
Criminal Code
development in the law. Our traditional British system of justice when compared with other systems in the world-and one has to recognize them as fair in themselves-more than the civil law system and other systems I have looked at tends to exclude evidence which tells the trier of fact that certain matters cannot be taken into account.
In many other systems the approach is different. In such other systems the court is allowed to consider evidence that is relevant and to say what weight it should be given. The Bill before us seems to be moving more toward a system in which formerly inadmissible evidence will be considered while the question of what weight it should be given will be raised.
I also have some reservations about the sufficient intelligence test that the Minister proposes be maintained in the law. While I agree that a judge ought to assess the capacity of a young person to tell a story as it happened-something about which the judge will have to make some judgment-"sufficient intelligence" is a test that has already been looked at by the courts. If one looks at the leading case in the field, Horsberg v. The Queen which dates back to 1968, one will see that the sufficient intelligence test boils down to a requirement that the complainant be of above-average intelligence. This is a case which went to the Supreme Court of Canada. The aboveaverage intelligence standard is a high standard. It is applicable to less than one-half of the people in a given group. It means that more than one-half of the children who might otherwise be complainants will fail the test. A great many cases that ought to be brought forward will not be brought forward.
While a judge ought to look at the intelligence of the complainant to apply the sufficient intelligence test, according to legal precedent this will result in the exclusion of a great deal of evidence rather than in its admissibility. This is subject to the question of how much weight is given to the evidence of the young person who tells a story and who is intelligent enough to be able to put forward a story that he or she believes to be true and that reflects a proper recollection of the incidents alleged to constitute a crime. This is a test which I will want to look at in the committee.
I would now like to deal with the removal of other traditional safeguards recommended in the Bill. First, there is the removal of the warning that the judge traditionally gives in the case of even formerly admissible evidence by a young person to the trier of fact that it is evidence of a young person and that the trier of fact must be extra careful in considering it. This warning will not be necessary in the future under the regime to be established by the legislation which is before us. I think that is a positive move.
The admission of videotape evidence taken soon after an incident occurs is an extremely important and welcome addition to the law. This means that shortly after the commission of an offence, the young person will be able to tell the story on videotape. I ask parenthetically why there could not be provision to have the story placed on sound tape. There may be some circumstances in which video cameras are not
available and where evidence could be given on an ordinary tape recording. Videotape gives the trier of fact an extra dimension in which to make judgments. One can watch the demeanor of the child telling the story. This helps one to conclude whether or not the child has been truthful and accurate. However, as I have said, video equipment may not always be available. If we are to trust a judge or a jury to make a judgment about the truthfulness of the evidence of a child then a sound recording may be useful. This is one of the issues on which we will question the expert witnesses who appear in committee to see whether or not such a provision can be added. From the stories I have heard from people who practise in this field, four or five years can go by between the time an offence is committed and the time the accused is found guilty or not. Thus videotaping a complainant at a time closer to the incident will reflect more accurately the vocabulary and life experience of a child. The evidence a child gives in court will be much different four or five years later because of the evolution of the child, because of his or her greater understanding of the sexual behaviour of adults and because of his or her own sexuality. That in itself is an argument for admitting a videotape or some other similarly recorded earlier recollection.
The provision with respect to the videotape calls for it to be made soon after the incident complained of. 1 wish to suggest that perhaps a videotape should be made soon after the child reveals the commission of an offence. Sometimes a period of time goes by before a child who has been subjected to the conduct about which he or she complains reports it. Again, there may be other intervals between the time of complaint and the time of trial. To limit videotaping to soon after the incident occurs will exclude videotape evidence in a case in which a child waits a year or two before deciding to complain about certain behaviour. I wish to discuss in committee the opening of a window for videotaping not only soon after the incident occurs, as is presently proposed, but soon after the disclosure or the making of a complaint by a young person. In general, I think that videotaping of this nature, or any taping, will enhance the ability of the court to make a proper decision.
I now wish to speak about the exclusion of the accused from the courtroom, which is unprecedented in our system of justice. The argument for exclusion is that the complainant when giving evidence in court could be intimidated while he or she is doing so while the accused is sitting in the same room, glaring, as he or she is entitled to do, at the young person in the witness box. The thought is that if the accused is removed then the young person might feel more free to tell the story. One could say the same about other people around the accused. In many cases, as in incest cases, for example, there might be other adults present in the courtroom whose presence could be intimidating to the young person. If this power is to be given, we ought to see if the judge might also have the power to exclude others who, by being present in the court while the young person is telling the story, might prevent the young person from feeling comfortable about telling the entire story.
November 4, 1986

Let us look at this from the other side for a moment. Nothing would be worse than developing a regime under which an accused would be denied a fair opportunity to defend himself or herself. What is the impact on the court of removing the accused and perhaps a larger group of people during testimony? I believe it is very prejudicial. If I were sitting on a jury and the accused was ordered by the judge to leave the courtroom along with others because of his or her demeanour,
I would find it pretty prejudicial. It might also damage the ability of the accused to defend himself.
The statute calls for the video taping of the procedure so that somehow or other, the accused will know what is going on in the courtroom while he is away and will be able to instruct counsel or respond to counsel. The machinery that is proposed here is a radical innovation. While 1 welcome it and believe it will achieve the basic goal of the Official Opposition, which is to see more of these cases come before the court and be dealt with by the court, we want to be fair as well. We want to be certain that the machinery the Government has in mind will not prejudice a jury or a trier of fact and will not tend to lead to convictions in cases where the accused has a defence and is innocent.
What I am about to say applies to this particular provision as well as to some of the other provisions. There are other jurisdictions in the world that are trying all these different methods. I do not think there is anything in this legislation, new and radical as it is for Canada, that has not been tried elsewhere.
It is not good enough for the Government to defend a procedure by saying that it has been tried elsewhere. We need to know how it has worked where it has been tried. In connection with divorce reform, some of the measures that were brought forward were called terrific by the Government because they had been tried elsewhere, but we heard evidence from elsewhere that it was not working as well as the Government had hoped it would work here.
In fairness to future accused and in the desire for fair trials, we want to know how these measures have worked where they have been tried. Have they been beneficial, have they resulted in miscarriages of justice or have they resulted in decisions acceptable to the population, decisions that provided a deterrent to the community and showed that young people are being protected by the courts of the land? Have these measures shown that certain kinds of behaviour will be punished and that there is a greater risk than there had once been of this type of behaviour being found out and dealt with by the courts?
The final issue with which I would like to deal regarding the reduction of safeguards is the matter of prior sexual activity. In the areas of sexual assault and aggravated sexual assault, the former Government of which I was a part led a move away from evidence of prior sexual activity being brought forward to prejudice the court against a complaint in rape cases. All of us
Criminal Code
at the bar know that the development of the law had been so regrettable and unfortunate that a woman with a certain kind of prior sexual behaviour could never bring a complaint before a court. Nothing that was done to her of which she would complain would result in a conviction because of the prejudice created by her former sexual behaviour. That was an unacceptable development of the law and it was important to make a move that permitted anyone who was raped, whatever her prior sexual behaviour, to bring forward a complaint and to obtain justice in the courts of the land.
In the legislation before us, the Government is proposing in proposed Section 246.6 that no evidence shall be adduced by or on behalf of the accused concerning the sexual activity of the complainant with any person other than the accused. Again, I welcome this provision but I want to be certain that we will not be moving too far in a direction which will prevent relevant evidence from coming before the trier of fact so that he may deal with the question of its weight. How much can one safeguard the truth while still allowing for a wide latitude in the admissibility of evidence that is logically relevant?
There is a lot in this Bill. It is very important that we move it forward. It is important that there be tougher laws in this area designed to punish offenders who target young people and abuse them sexually. I hope that the process of Parliament will work quickly. I would like to assure the Minister of my cooperation. However, I must note that the Minister's predecessor had a very poor track record with the legislation that was brought forward.
I can name chapter and verse a number of the Bills that were brought through the House, and I would if the Minister were here, which have been struck down as violating the Charter. I believe it behooves all of us to take more care than the Government has taken to date of the Charter implications and the requirements of the Charter for fair trials, free speech and free access. We do not want to see the Government continue to abuse the Charter and the goal of the Charter which is to enhance the rights and freedoms of Canadians. That kind of concern which has not meant much to the Government so far must mean a great deal to the Opposition.
When we deal with legislation, as important as it is, we do not want to see the Conservative tendency which one also sees in the United States toward having pious declarations become legislation and particularly criminal legislation for which people may be convicted and serve time. We do not want to translate a public sentiment into a criminal statute. We do want to respond to a public sentiment and, within our traditions of fairness, free speech and all the other rights and freedoms we enjoy in Canada, we do want to try to advance society and protect young people and women, but at the same time we want to do this in a way that is consistent with the fundamental freedoms that make this a liberal democracy. However often Canadians rally for a drastic solution to a problem, when cases come before the courts as a result of drastic sentiments, they want the people who appear before the courts of Canada to have fair treatment.

November 4, 1986
Criminal Code

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE AND CANADA EVIDENCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to participate in the debate on this very important piece of legislation, Bill C-15. It is important and long overdue legislation designed to deal with the hidden tragedy of child abuse.
It was in August of 1984 that the Badgley Commission submitted its report to the Government documenting what it termed "a national crisis" of the sexual abuse of young people. There has been debate and considerable discussion since that time as to the actual extent of child sexual abuse, and the extent to which it may be a phenomenon which is increasing in our society, or merely one which is being reported in increasing numbers. Nevertheless, no Member of this House can deny that we all have an obligation to deal quickly and effectively with this tragedy.
The Badgley Commission recommendations were tabled in August of 1984. Shortly after that I called upon the newly elected Government to move forward and take action to deal with the concerns that were raised by that commission, not necessarily to implement all of the recommendations chapter and verse by any means, but to recognize that a problem does exist and it is one that should be addressed. It took the Government over a year before it even began to respond to the recommendations of the Badgley Commission.
Approximately one year later, in August of 1985, the ministry embarked upon a series of consultations. These consultations were rushed so much that many of the groups consulted strongly protested the nature and the process of the consultations. They were also concerned that the Department of National Health and Welfare was not involved in those negotiations, and certainly should have been.
Following those consultations the Government introduced two Bills last June. This is once again a lag of almost another year. It is a matter of considerable regret that in the concern that was expressed, in my view quite properly with respect to the companion Bill C-114 on pornography, many of the important questions raised by the legislation on child sexual abuse were completely ignored.
Quite understandably, the press focused on the repressive and Neanderthal provisions of Bill C-114, the pornography legislation, and completely ignored many of the provisions dealing with child sexual abuse in Bill C-113. Much of the important focus and concern that had been raised at the time of the tabling of the Badgley Commission Report was lost in the publicity and the concern over pornography legislation.
I am pleased that the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) has decided to move forward with the child abuse legislation separate and apart from Bill C-114, the pornography legislation. If it is his intention to bring forward similar legislation to that brought forward by his colleague, the now Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), I would suggest that he delay that as long as he possibly can because it certainly will
meet with vigorous resistance from many Members in this House.
That is not to say that we in this Party believe that action is not necessary to deal with the present archaic laws in Canada on pornography. Clearly such action is needed, particularly in the area of violent pornography and pornography which is degrading. To suggest that we take the sweeping approach to stomping out any depiction of consensual adults sexual activity, as advocated by many of the Minister's colleagues, is surely an approach that we cannot accept.
I would suggest to all Members of this House that they go back two or three years and review the proceedings of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs in dealing with similar legislation on pornography and sexual abuse of young people. That legislation was Bill C-53. The present Minister of Justice spoke at that time to the Justice Committee with considerable force and eloquence against the proposals of the previous Government in Bill C-53. I intend, in the course of the deliberations on this legislation before the Justice Committee, which I understand will be dealing with this legislation, to remind the Minister and his colleagues on that committee of the position that he took at that time on that legislation. I hope that perhaps, with that consistency for which he is so well known, he will in fact adopt a similar position in response to amendments that I intend to put forward to this legislation.
The Badgley Commission documented a very disturbing human tragedy involving young people in Canada. It is a largely hidden tragedy, as I indicated earlier. The scars of the sexual abuse of young people can be borne for a lifetime. Too often the abuse of young people is then in turn repeated, and that vicious cycle is continued. The Minister referred earlier to this. This is a cycle which we must make every possible effort to break. Clearly there can be debate as to the actual extent of child sexual abuse in Canada. There are those who argue that the estimates by the Badgley Commission are excessive and unreasonable. Whatever the extent, it is clear that this Parliament must take firm and effective action now to deal with that crisis.
Clearly changes in the law are required. There is no doubt about that. I intend to comment on the Minister's specific proposals.
I believe it is also essential that we recognize that changes in the law alone are totally inadequate to deal with this serious problem. Indeed, changes in the criminal law may in fact result in a significantly larger number of people coming into direct contact with the criminal justice system. If the additional resources are not put in place to deal with those individuals-here I speak both of victims and offenders-then we will be doing a disservice and not a service to the victims of sexual abuse.
There must be a clear recognition of the need for significantly enhanced resources both provincially and federally to deal with the problem of child sexual abuse. We have to look at the
November 4, 1986

prevention as well as the assisting of victims of child sexual abuse and resources to treat offenders, those who would abuse the children themselves sexually. I have spoken about the victims of child sexual abuse. It is important to note that there are also adult survivors who bear the scars of sexual abuse that they may have suffered as children. There must be resources to assist the adult survivors of sexual abuse to cope with those problems and overcome the scars and the pain which they have suffered. In short, we have to attempt to break that cycle of child sexual abuse which is so pervasive.
In this regard, it is essential to note that many of the resouces which should be in place are seriously lacking. Many of the legislative provisions at the provincial level are seriously lacking. I believe that there are only four provinces, four jurisdictions, which even include sexual abuse as part of their definition of children in need of protection in their child protection statutes. Clearly that must change. While we cannot rewrite provincial legislation, we can certainly send a strong signal of our concerns.
It is also important that we look at the enhanced provision of services for abused children. There are many omissions in this area. There is duplication of effort, the absence of effective coordination between service programs, and ineffective evaluation of whether policy initiatives, guidelines, and programs are actually working and benefiting children. Too often provincial jurisdictions are not putting the amount of money into this problem that they should be. Too often professionals that work in the field are not paying the type of attention that they should be.
In a paper in which Lorenne Clark did a critique of the Badgley Report she stated:
-how is one to make sense of the fact that most jurisdictions do not even recognize sexual abuse of children as behaviour constituting a sufficient condition for declaring a child to be a child in need of protection, that the agencies dealing with the problem do not even know whether the guidelines they are following and the programs they have developed either work or benefit those for whom they are intended, and do not function either as major direct recipients of complaints or even as frequently utilized referrals, and that in two-thirds of the sexual abuse cases coming to them, they themselves may have contributed to that abuse because their belief in the importance of keeping the families of these victims intact led them to refrain from intervention when they already knew that sexual abuse had taken place?
We have illustrations from across Canada about the absence of resources. In Halifax, Children's Aid Society workers now deal with about 50 cases each. This is a far too heavy case load. There is a three month waiting period for psychological treatment of sexual abuse. Similar inadequacies have been documented across the country in the summary of the consultations prepared by Neville Avison of the federal Ministry of Justice. I should like to quote what I think Mr. Avison said very well in his report. He said:
It was believed to be useless, or even worse than useless, for the federal Government to address the legal concerns without having-plans being implemented for the infrastructure of programs and services that would be required.
Criminal Code
I strongly support that statement. We need resources at both provincial and federal levels. There must be an effective coordination of the involvement of the federal Government in this area. For that reason I very much regret that the Ministry of National Health and Welfare has not played a higher profile or a more active role in the whole question of dealing with child sexual abuse.
It was in June of this year that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) said that the Government would be announcing shortly the appointment of a special adviser on child sexual abuse. He said that there would be committees of regional advisers as well. One can debate whether there should be a special adviser reporting to the Minister or a commissioner reporting to the Prime Minister as Badgley recommended. However, what surely should be beyond debate is the suggestion that the Government should move quickly to ensure that there is an effective co-ordination of the response of the federal Government in this area. The Minister said in June of this year that the Government would be announcing shortly the appointment of this special adviser. It is now November and we are still waiting. Five months later and the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who is unable to join us in the debate this morning, has failed to act on the promise which he made to move forward with an effective co-ordinating body. I would hope the Minister would recognize his responsibilities and take action on this matter immediately.
As well, the Minister of National Health and Welfare announced with great fanfare that the Government intended to spend the sum of $20 million over five years to deal with the whole question of child sexual abuse. The evidence is clear that such an amount is a pittance and falls far short of what is necessary to respond effectively to the concerns of those who are active in the field of child sexual abuse. That $20 million is approximately half the amount the Government is wasting on the construction of a federal penitentiary at Port-Cartier in the Province of Quebec. The total amount the Government is prepared to commit to child sexual abuse is half the amount being wasted on the construction of a federal penitentiary in the riding of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). It is shameful that the Government is not prepared to spend more money or to put more resources into effectively dealing with the concerns surrounding child sexual abuse.
A former employee of the Department of National Health and Welfare, Dr. Susan Painter, who worked for that Department from 1981 to 1984 as director of an information service on family violence, has said that she does not understand why her former Department has not responded. She said:
I don't see any excuse for the lack of action.
She is right, and it is about time the Minister of National Health and Welfare recognized his responsibility in this area and realized that a legal response is simply not good enough.
I would note, in closing on this particular point, that Mr. Neville Avison commented in his summary of the discussions following national consultations that those attending the

November 4, 1986
Criminal Code
discussions regretted the absence of a National Health and Welfare representative from the discussion team. Once again we see the colleague of the Minister of Justice failing to fulfil his responsibilities to the children of Canada ana failing to play an active role in this important area.
We must look at the whole question of social services, but we must recognize as well that there is a more fundamental and basic question which we as a society must address-the whole question of male socialization in society. It has been pointed out that over 98 per cent of the offenders in the area of child sexual abuse are males, are men. It is men who are the pimps. It is men who are overwhelmingly the consumers of pornography. It is men who are the customers of prostitutes. Until we can attack in a very fundamental way the socialization which leads to this phenomenon of men being the abusers, the users, and the customers, surely we will not have come to grips with the problem of child sexual abuse or discrimination against women and children.
Again it was Lorenne Clark who wrote very eloquently about this particular matter in the paper to which I referred earlier. I should like to note briefly her comments. She said:
Sexual response is a learned behaviour, and until men can accept themselves as the equals rather than the superiors of women, and can learn new sexual responses appropriate to that status, most aspects of the problem will remain unchanged.
The Church Council on Justice and Corrections, in its brief to the Minister, noted that there was a societal problem in the socialization process of young males. Until recently women and children were considered to be subjected to the power and authority of their husbands and fathers, with very few rights of their own. Women have now acquired legal rights by law and are starting to have these rights respected, but to attribute rights to children is a very recent concept. It is still revolutionary to say that children are not the property of their fathers but are citizens with equal rights to respect and dignity. In that regard I note that it was the former Hon. Member for St. John's East who introduced a Bill into the House in 1978 proposing a Bill of rights for children. I introduced similar legislation, and I believe that approach is one at which we as Members should look with considerable care.
In looking at the whole question of the sexual abuse of young people and children, we recognize a serious concern in society. However, I believe it is very important that in focusing as we are today on the sexual abuse of young children, we not lose sight of other forms of abuse of children. There is a danger that if we as a society focus upon the sexual abuse of young people, we will not give the attention which is warranted to other forms of violence and abuse of children.
In 1959, Canada was one of the signatories to the United Nations Declaration of the Rights of the Child. That Declaration set out very clearly that the child shall enjoy special protection and shall be given opportunities and facilities, in law and by other means, to enable him to develop physically, mentally, morally, spiritually, and socially in a healthy and normal manner and in conditions of freedom and dignity. We
as a society have fallen far short if that is to be our benchmark, as I suggest it should. We have not come to grips with the problem of physical abuse of children, and I am not speaking here of sexual abuse. We have not come to grips with the battering of children which was so clearly documented by the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs in its 1981 report. We must recognize that that is a serious concern we must address. Surely we must ask ourselves whether it is really appropriate that we should in effect be tolerating child abuse explicitly in the provisions of the Criminal Code of Canada. In its 1981 report, in referring to Section 43 of the Criminal Code, the committee indicated:
The Criminal Code as it now stands provides a legal framework for child abuse.
I remind Hon. Members that it is Section 43 of the Criminal Code which indicates explicitly that schoolteachers, parents, and those who stand in the place of parents can in fact use what is called "force" against children.
Why? Why is it that we as a society are prepared to tolerate the use of force against those who are the weakest and most helpless in society, when we will not allow the use of force against any other citizen in our community? It used to be that we would allow the use of force against women, who were seen as appendages or chattels of their husbands. Fortunately those days are gone, but we as a society still tolerate the use of force and violence against our children. I believe, and I speak now as an individual and not on behalf of my party, that the time has come for us to re-evaluate this question. We have to ask ourselves very seriously whether we should not be adopting a fundamentally different approach to the way we treat our children. In Sweden, following lengthy study and debate, the law was changed to prohibit use of physical punishment against children. The law now reads that a child may not be subjected to physical punishment or other injurious or humiliating treatment. The time has come for us to examine very carefully whether that is not an appropriate response for us as a society. After all, what is the dividing line between a spanking and a beating? Who makes that very important decision?
We also have to look at the extent of violence on television. The reality is that a child exposed to television over a number of years will probably have seen something like 18,000 deaths by the time he or she reaches the age of 18. Our movies are full of violence. Video games encourage children to kill as many creatures as possible, as quickly as possible. I am sure that leads to attitudes which can in turn generate violence.
Then there is the violence of poverty itself. The National Council on Child Welfare documented this problem very eloquently. We have the poverty and violence of hunger and cold. We have poverty and violence which leads to young native people drinking photocopier fluid and dying, as happened in Peerless Lake, Alberta. Surely we must not overlook these other forms of abuse and violence of our
November 4, 1986

children which leads to teenage suicides in record numbers in some of our provinces. As Jeffrey Wilson, an author who has written extensively about the position of young people in our society, said, too often the modern reality of Canadian childhood includes the shopping mall, the street corner, the teenage drug abuser, the child suicide, the AWOL kids, struggling in our cities to find a job, a fake ID and a warm place to sleep for the night. That is the reality of too many children in Canada today.
This legislation deals with a number of concerns in this area. It deals with evidentiary provisions which would make it easier to prosecute child sexual abuse in Canada. It would make it easier for children to give evidence. It deals with substantive law in the Criminal Code and there are provisions dealing with juvenile prostitution. Allow me to refer briefly to the clauses in the legislation dealing with juvenile prostitution.
In March of 1983, the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General considered the whole area of prostitution. It did not agree on many things. In fact, there was only one issue on which all three Parties in this House agreed. That was, that the Criminal Code of Canada should be amended to provide sanctions explicitly against those who would attempt to purchase the sexual services of young people. We supported that suggestion in 1983. We have since advocated that the Government move on that suggestion. Certainly we are pleased to see the legislation before the House today incorporate that important provision. I am also pleased to note that the Government rejected the recommendations of the Badgley Commission in that respect.
I see the Hon. Member for Outremont (Mrs. Pepin) has just entered the House. She served with distinction as a member of the Badgley Commission. I say to her that while there were many important provisions in that report, the suggestion that young people be charged as criminals for engaging in acts of prostitution is one that I believe this Government quite properly rejected. However, the Government went on to deal with prostitution in a manner which many of us felt to be completely inappropriate, and Bill C-49 was adopted in the last session of this House despite the opposition of both opposition Parties. That Bill in effect made life even more difficult for young people on the street involved in acts of prostitution. It has driven them underground and in some cases has made them more dependent on pimps. David Dranchuk, who has worked extensively on the streets of Vancouver with juvenile prostitutes, pointed out that since this Bill was enacted the lot of juvenile prostitutes is worse than it was before. We warned the Government of that, and unfortunately the warning has turned into a harsh reality. I hope the Government recognizes that that approach was wrong. It flew in the face of the recommendations of the Fraser Committee and certainly it contributed to the expansion rather than the reduction of child sexual abuse.
Dealing with the two major areas of this Bill, I would like to touch on the evidentiary provisions. My friend from York Centre has already referred to a number of the proposed
Criminal Code
changes, as has the Minister himself. Surely the fundamental principle must be that we allow the child to tell his or her story clearly in court without any sense of intimidation. Does this Bill facilitate that objective? It would eliminate the present requirement for corroboration. We welcome that and we will support it in committee. It is quite unfair that under the present law, if a child cannot be sworn and there is no corroboration, the case must be thrown out of court. That has been a significant barrier to dealing effectively with child sexual abuse in the courts.
However, the provisions as presently drafted fall significantly short of what we believe should be the case. The governing principle should be to facilitate communication by the child. There should not be a test of sufficient intelligence, as proposed in this Bill. We have already seen that the interpretation of this test has led to unreasonable expectations. One judge said it is not good enough to have just average intelligence, the child must be above average in intelligence. Yet, it should not be the intelligence of the child that governs, it should be the ability of that child to communicate to the court that governs. Surely judges should be able to weigh the evidence.
I suggest as well that children be allowed to use devices which might assist them in communicating. A young child, for example, might wish to use an anatomically correct doll to explain exactly what has happened to him or her. I believe that should be permitted by the courts.
The provisions with respect to videotaping evidence are a step forward. The drafting of this provisions leaves something to be desired, however. I believe videotaping should be allowed not just shortly after the offence, because in some cases the child is afraid to speak and it is only after several weeks or months that it finally has the courage to speak out. I would suggest that shortly after the disclosure of the offence the videotaping should be permitted. Nor is it good enough just to permit videotaping. I suggest a record in another form, perhaps an audio recording, is appropriate as well. If this is to work effectively there must be the fundamental safeguard of allowing the accused to watch the evidence of the child and comment on it to his or her lawyer. There are obviously many parts of the country in which there are not adequate resources to facilitate such videotaping of evidence. I suggest that the federal Government should assist in providing those resources.
There are also concerns about the provisions with respect to decorum in the court room and the exclusion of the public from the court room. It may very well be that there should be provisions for the exclusion of the public at the discretion of the judge when a young person is testifying. There are a number of other evidentiary provisions which we will want to examine carefully in the course of committee study.
The Canadian Council on Children and Youth has made a number of important recommendations for changes, as has the Metropolitan Toronto Special Committee on Child Abuse. I

November 4, 1986
Criminal Code
hope that they will be given an opportunity to appear before the committee and make representations in the area of the presentation of evidence. One area in this Bill which I would emphasize as being of fundamental importance, aside from the substantive offences which I will deal with shortly, is the question of evidence. We are concerned that the proposals fall dramatically short of what is appropriate for ensuring that children's evidence gets before the courts.
There are lawyers, particularly defence counsel, who have various concerns about these provisions. Harold Levy, the editor of the Criminal Lawyers Association Newsletter, has called these changes "incredibly dangerous". I have a great deal of respect for Harold Levy. He said:
There seems to be a "believe-the-children movement" which is tied into the children's-rights issue. But they don't have the right to be believed just because they are children.
I fundamentally disagree with that. The fact is that under the law as it now stands children are disbelieved just because they are children. It is about time we recognized that children do have the right to be heard and we should be taking the necessary steps in law to facilitate that right.
The last portion of the Bill which I would like to address contains the substantive provisions of the legislation, the new offences which are created in this Bill. This is obviously an area of the law which is in serious need of overhaul. The Badgely Commission and the Fraser Commission documented offences which are not covered by the existing provisions of the Criminal Code. Similarly, there are other actions which are presently criminalized which should not be the subject of criminal sanction. I would like to address both of those areas in the few minutes I have remaining for making my remarks today.
There are some serious weaknesses and inequities in the substantive offence provisions of this Bill. The Bill refers to "sexual touching" and creates offences for that. Sexual touching is not defined in the legislation. I realize that it is difficult to define that with precision, but I suggest that the committee should try to formulate an appropriate definition of "sexual touching". If it does not, there is greater potential for abuse of this, particularly by law enforcement authorities who may define as "sexual touching" conduct which none of us in this House would reasonably believe should fall under that particular description.
The Bill would, as well, criminalize adolescent sexual behaviour which is currently not the subject of criminal sanctions. As the Canadian Council on Children and Youth has pointed out, under the present law we do not criminalize the acts of a 14-year old who may be necking and petting with a 13-year old or the actions of two 13-year olds who happen to be fooling around or engaging in sexual activity or experimentation. No one in the House is suggesting that we should take steps to indicate our approval of teenage sexual activity. However, the reality that young people under the age of 16 do engage in sexual experimentation must be faced. This Bill would criminalize that sexual experimentation amoung young
people. I suggest that education at home, school, church and elsewhere is the best way for children to develop in a sexually healthy and mature fashion. We should not use the sledgehammer of criminal law against sexual experimentation and activity between adolescents.
The Bill is curious in that it would say that it is okay for a 13-year old and a 12-year old to engage in adolescent sexual experimentation. However, for a 14-year old and a 13-year old to engage in the same kind of sexual experimentation is a criminal offence. That makes no sense whatever. I suggest that we study very seriously the recommendations of the Canadian Council on Children and Youth in this area.
In addition, the Bill would single out for special treatment under the Criminal Code the offence of buggery. It would reduce the age from 21 to 18 but would maintain the offence of buggery for special treatment. The Special Committee on Equality Rights recommended that there should be a uniform age of consent for homosexual and heterosexual activity. I suggest that by retaining the offence of buggery and applying an age of consent of 18 to it, the Government continues to discriminate against young gays. I suggest that the committee may want to examine as well the term "buggery".
In reality, in dealing with the offence of buggery the Government is saying that two 17-year olds, including two 17-year olds of the same sex, for example, cannot engage in an act of anal intercourse but may engage in any other form of sexual activity. If the Government wants to justify this form of discrimination, surely it will have to demonstrate to the committee that this conduct is more harmful than heterosexual conduct or other homosexual conduct in the same age group. I suggest that in the absence of the ability to demonstrate that, the legislation should apply a uniform age of consent.
I note as well that the legislation attempts to lower the age of consent from 21 to 18 for buggery. However, at the same time there is a quite pejorative reference to consent by individuals who are "feeble-minded, insane, an idiot or imbecile". I suggest that maintaining that kind of language in the Criminal Code is quite inappropriate. I hope the committee would redraft that language if it is to be maintained at all.
I suggest that in the absence of compelling evidence the committee should adopt the recommendation of a uniform age of consent.
In conclusion, I would like to emphasize that we in this Party recognize that this subject must be addressed with care and in depth by Parliament and, in particular, by the committee which will be established to consider the legislation. It requires careful study. We have co-operated in ensuring that the debate on second reading of this Bill came forward quickly.
I hope that the Minister recognizes that there must be adequate time for those groups involved in this issue to be able to prepare their responses to the legislation and appear before the committee. I hope the Government will ensure that there are adequate resources to assist them in appearing before the committee.
November 4, 1986

The legislation before us is of fundamental importance. We in the New Democratic Party are prepared to give it very serious and responsible consideration. I hope the Government will recognize that the changes which I suggested would make this a better Bill which all members of the House could support.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francois Gerin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE AND CANADA EVIDENCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I wish to congratulate the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) on tabling this Bill so soon. I also wish to reiterate his request that all Canadians support the fight against child sexual abuse. This request was made earlier by the Minister to the Opposition parties, and I was happy to hear spokespersons for the two Opposition parties give the House the assurance it would have their full co-operation for speedy passage of these measures.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister sought this co-operation not only because he believes in these measures as the Minister of Justice of Canada, but also because two important committees made the same request previously. The Badgley Report and the Fraser Report both recognized that the problem was an urgent one and required a joint effort by all levels of government in Canada and by all other social agencies and organizations in our society. The Badgley Committee submitted a total of 52 recommendations addressed to all levels of government and to the private sector. They contain a wide range of approaches, including heightening the awareness of society, public education, improving public health and amendments to criminal law. The Badgley proposals specifically identify two preconditions. First of all, to deal effectively with the personal and social ills arising from child sexual abuse will require concerted action on the part of all levels of our society. Second, the Government of Canada must play a central role in this action. Consequently, it is only logical that the Canadian Government should use criminal law to fight against certain kinds of behaviour that cause considerable harm to others and that it should involve special social and educational measures in the process. While the federal Government can play a major role at the national level and continue to make the public aware of these issues, we must remember that under the Canadian Constitution, the responsibility for providing social and health services to Canadians lies with the provinces. The federal Government will therefore act as a catalyst in this area and seek the co-operation of the provinces in dealing with these issues.
The key to the success of this new program which is aimed at fighting child sexual abuse will be to obtain the co-operation of all levels of government and the private sector. These problems must therefore be addressed, first and foremost, at the local level, and we hope that in future, the provinces will help the federal Government to identify areas where concerted action could be taken. I am convinced that this Government
Criminal Code
also intends to maintain and even strengthen its close relationship with the many volunteer organizations involved in this field. Private sector participation is a must as well. We are aware that in many instances these organizations are in an ideal position to take quick and appropriate community action.
This Bill deals with several major issues, Mr. Speaker, but I am pleased that the Government has seen fit to dissociate it from the legislative measure on pornography. It would have been unfortunate had all these Criminal Code amendments been lumped together, for Bill C-15 would have lost its impact and the special consideration it deserves precisely because it excludes other measures related to pornography. As a matter of fact there is no doubt that within a few weeks- recently the Minister of Justice did express the hope that the Bill might be introduced before Christmas-the Bill on pornography will come up for reconsideration which will not include these provisions respecting sexual abuse of young children.
Among other points, Mr. Speaker, I intend to deal today with specific amendments related to the Canada Evidence Act.
As a criminal lawyer with over 15 years' experience I paid special attention to the amendments concerning corroboration, testimony by the spouse, failure of the accused to attend when a child gives evidence, in certain cases, admissibility of videotaped evidence, lack of recent complaint and extension of the limitation period.
This week, Mr. Speaker, I heard about and read certain articles dealing mainly with the question of corroboration. This rule, which is very familiar to judges and lawyers alike, caused many problems to prosecutors and much satisfaction to lawyers for the defense. In my opinion, this is an exceptional rule. Why require corroboration of the evidence of a child if you do not require the same corroboration in the case of evidence given by a very old person or someone whose evidence before the court is rather incoherent.
In such cases, the usual rules of evidence apply, which means that the evidence is judged on its own merits. Who is in a better position to evaluate evidence than the judge or members of the jury? Who could be in a better position than these twelve men and women to decide whether evidence should be believed totally, partly or not at all, whether it is given by a 40 year-old or a 10 year-old?
It seems to me that most jury members are Canadians with children of their own, and they are aware of the problems which can result when a child tells his own version of the facts. Parents are able to understand, judge and assess what a child has said and generality to decide whether he should be believed completely, partly or not at all, just as jury members do in all cases before the courts in Canada by listening to the evidence of the witness, whoever he may be.
I am very happy about this new rule which removes the need for corroboration, and as a defence lawyer, it does not scare me. I am convinced that other defence lawyers will be able, through an appropriate cross-interrogation, that the judges will be able, thanks to their usual wisdom, and that the jury

November 4, 1986
Criminal Code
members will be able, thanks to what they see happening before their eyes and their own common sense, to decide what credence should be given to the evidence of a child.
I am not worried at all. I have myself been much more concerned when I saw frightened young children give evidence not knowing whether they should say that they knew what the Bible was or what the nature of the oath was, not taking the oath and afterwards giving their evidence quite coherently and credibly, and when J then saw, because of this corroboration rule, the judge often say publicly at the hearing that, regretfully, he could not accept the evidence of these children because it had not been corroborated on an essential point involving the accused. Then, the accused was acquitted on a technicality. Canadians find this unacceptable. So do the parents of these young children. Generally, this is viewed as unacceptable by our society, where there have been some changes in attitudes that we should recognize today. Mr. Speaker, such corroboration is no longer necessary in 1986. Nowadays, it is replaced by the normal rules of evidence, which normally determine how you should judge evidence.
As a defence lawyer, I am not at all worried about the accused. They may not be acquitted on technicalities, but they can still be acquitted if they are able, by effective crossinterrogation or other evidence, to weaken or undermine the evidence of the child, as that of any other witness. This is the fair solution.
The presiding judge at a trial by jury will no longer have to advise the members of the jury to be careful before condemning an accused on the evidence of a child. This will no longer be necessary. However, in any trial by jury, the judge must explain thoroughly the nature of the evidence and what the jury members must do before deciding whether a witness should be believed completely, partly or not at all. He must explain this well. In any case, my personal experience has always been that the jury members' just as anyone else who follows a trial closely, make up their minds about the quality of a witness and of his evidence. There is therefore no reason for concern about this either.
By the way, 1 want to say that I am also delighted that the legislation should no longer discriminate between young girls and young boys. 1 think it is a very good change. This is indeed a practical application of the political speeches and promises made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in 1984, reiterated in the first Throne Speech, and reiterated again recently in the last Throne Speech. This is an example with practical application in our daily life. 1 suggest all Hon. Member should congratulate the Government for this new legislation.
There is also an amendment to the Canada Evidence Act which would now allow or even compel the spouse of an accused to testify when the victim is a child of the accused. That is normal. In many cases, that might be the only testimony. A mother might be aware of a fact and could not tell it to the judge, because of a particular provision in the legislation which generally made it possible for the accused to
say: I do not want my wife to come and testify against me. This is a time honoured tradition which all Canadians will accept to break in the case of sexual offences against children.
Mr. Speaker, a provision of this Bill which will make it possible for the presiding judge or justice, under special circumstances and following an investigation, to exclude the accused during the testimony of a child, will certainly create a whole new jurisprudence. It obviously raises a number of practical problems, as in the case of an accused who would defend himself.
Clearly, the Legislative Committee will have to study this provision closely and consider its application to various cases. Yet, as counsel for the defence, I also put a lot of trust on the intelligence of the presiding judges who will be called upon to determine exactly when this very special provision should apply. I firmly believe, for instance, that in the case of an accused who is defending himself, the justice would appreciate and decide each case on its merit.
In my opinion, that videotaped evidence should become admissible is excellent. Of course, in our courts, it often happens that proceeding commence only several months, if not several years, following the alleged offence. How could we ask a ten-year old child, for instance, to remember all the details two or three years after the alleged offence.
In practice, we used to try and refresh the child's memory by using a previous statement. From now on, this legislation will allow the courts to refresh the child's memory publicly and openly, and if the child is able to recognize his or her previous statement, this videotaped evidence will become admissible as proof. Again, that is an excellent change. This applies also to recent complaints which have always caused serious problems before our courts. The absence of prescription is also a very good thing. In fact, such a prescription exists under the Criminal Code for all offences punishable on summary conviction. It continues to exist. For indictable offences-it did not exist for other indictable offences and I do not see why it should exist in the case of a sexual offence against a child. No distinction should be made. That is a measure which is therefore more equitable.
The existing criminal law provisions contained a number of restrictions and I will single out a few, Mr. Speaker. Young boys and girls did not enjoy equal protection under the law. In many cases the victim had to be a female and the accused a male.
Most offences related exclusively to vaginal sexual intercourse and did not cover the wide variety of sexual activities which can be described as abuse of children such as touching, masturbation and oral-genital contacts against which young boys and girls alike must be protected.
There was also the Criminal Code legal presumption whereby a boy under 14 was deemed unable to maintain an erection and have sexual intercourse. This flies in the face of today's biological reality, Mr. Speaker.
November 4, 1986

The age of sexual consent varies under the existing Criminal Code provisions, but this will be changed according to the sexual act involved and the sex of the participant.
Mr. Speaker, I see that my time is running out. I wanted to make these few remarks on the amendments and tell you that this Bill is one of the social justice measureSTmveiled by the Government in the Speech from the Throne delivered less than a month ago. I invite all Canadians to familiarize themselves with these new rules and abide by them. I urge all my colleagues in the House, regardless of their Party, to support this Government endeavour which goes a long way to meet the wishes of the members of the Badgley and Fraser committees, as well as those of Canadians and parents throughout this country.
