subtopic: INCREASED RESIDENTIAL CONSTRUCTION
INCREASED RESIDENTIAL CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to report that our residential building industry continues to boom. This is just one more sign that the economic objectives of the Government are right on track. As quoted in The Globe and Mail of today:
Residential construction across Canada continues to outpace even the most optimistic forecasts-
"The spectacular strength of new home building-is breath-taking-
Up to September of this year national housing starts number almost 125,000-a 26 per cent increase over the same period last year. The figures are equally impressive for the Province of Ontario where there is a 29 per cent increase over last year's starts. However, this building upsurge carries right across the country. For example, the Province of Nova Scotia is ahead by a spectacular 50 per cent.
In my riding of Niagara Falls and the surrounding area housing starts are 34 per cent ahead of last year. This is good news for Niagara Falls and good news for all of Canada.

subtopic: CALL FOR ACCELERATION OF MANITOBA PROJECTS
CALL FOR ACCELERATION OF MANITOBA PROJECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Manitobans of all political stripes feel that a great injustice has been committed against our province. In the days and weeks ahead the Government will have ample opportunity to

November 4, 1986
address that injustice by making good on other decisions that will beneficially affect the Manitoba economy.
Specifically, the Government should act as soon as possible to implement the remaining two-thirds of the box-car rehabilitation program in Transcona; decide to build, and to build in Winnipeg, the new light-weight hopper-cars; proceed with the VIA Rail shop in Winnipeg; order the new transcontinental equipment for VIA; review its cancellation of the manufacturing technology centre; live up to its commitments to Churchill; reverse the shift of IRDP funds to central Canada; and reverse the cut-backs in federal transfer payments to the provinces, such as Manitoba, which are hardest hit.
In addition, the Government should also be looking for ways to prevent the unravelling of the aerospace industry in Winnipeg-a process begun by the Liberals a long time ago when they transferred the Air Canada overhaul base in Winnipeg to Montreal-instead of helping to unravel that industry further as it did last week.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT'S RECOGNITION OF WORK OF VOLUNTEERS
GOVERNMENT'S RECOGNITION OF WORK OF VOLUNTEERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the work of volunteers in our society has enriched the lives of those who participate in such services as well as the lives of those they help. The dedication of workers like Margaret Corbett, Helen Fennell, and Don MacLean from the riding of Welland has contributed greatly to the communities of South St. Catharines and Thorold.
Mr. MacLean has worked for many years organizing recreational sports. Mrs. Fennell has contributed years of work to the Canadian Cancer Society. Mrs. Corbett has been very active on behalf of severely mentally handicapped children. The two women were among 71 people across Canada to be awarded the Canada Volunteer Award Certificate of Merit this year.
I was pleased to hear in the Speech from the Throne that the Government plans further support for the growth of volunteer service in society. Recognition of the value of volunteers should be a priority of every level of government and of all Canadians.

subtopic: PARKER COMMISSION-PAYMENT OF FORMER MINISTER'S LEGAL EXPENSES
PARKER COMMISSION-PAYMENT OF FORMER MINISTER'S LEGAL EXPENSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I object to the Government's authorization of a payment of up to
$350,000 for the legal fees of the Hon. Member for York- Peel (Mr. Stevens) who is defending himself on violations of conflict of interest guidelines. I believe it is fair for the Government to pay the bills of a Minister who is defending the way he did his job and his behaviour as a Minister. However, in this case the allegations are that the Minister in effect engaged in moonlighting while he was a Minister.
I submit that it is not fair for a person who is defending himself on allegations of moonlighting to have his bills paid by the Government of Canada. There is no precedent for this of which I am aware, and I tried to find one. Any official of the Government who must defend his own conduct before a commission should have his fees paid, but not for doing things extraneous to the job.

RESULT OF PEMBINA BY-ELECTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the byelection in the Pembina riding held on September 29 was history in the making. The electors of Pembina demonstrated once again their confidence in the Progressive Conservative Party, the one most competent and best equipped to administer the affairs of our great country.

subtopic: PAROLE SUPERVISION PRIVATIZATION PROPOSAL
PAROLE SUPERVISION PRIVATIZATION PROPOSAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Department of the Solicitor General has recently privatized, without consultation, parole supervision for 250 parolees in Toronto to the John Howard Society. The mission of the Correctional Service to help offenders become law-abiding citizens is demeaned by shoving aside a professional workforce of highly skilled and deeply committed workers in favour of the employees of a largely voluntary organization. This change does no service to parolees and it does no service to the people of Canada who demand a professional supervision service.
November 4, 1986

Not only is the whole system of parole put into question by this ill-conceived move so too is the John Howard Society's role as one of the most important prisoner service organizations in Canada. Indeed, there is internal division on this question.
I call upon the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) to halt this mindless proposal immediately and to allow the Justice Committee to hold full hearings on it. As well, I would hope that the Government would ensure that there would be no reprisals against those public servants who had the courage to speak out against this senseless move toward privatization in the Correctional Service of Canada.

subtopic: CONSEQUENCES OF GOVERNMENT CUT-BACKS
CONSEQUENCES OF GOVERNMENT CUT-BACKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I should like to read in this House a letter sent to the Prime Minister of Canada by one of my constituents and I quote:
I have been an employee of the CNRC for six years. During that period, I have filed 14 industrial copyright applications for which permits have been purchased by three Canadian companies. I have also written 46 scientific papers and an internationally renowned book. I mention this to show that I am an aboveaverage researcher in Canada as elsewhere.
Due to the recent climate of uncertainty for applied research in this country, I am now considering going to work abroad. Unless conditions change drastically in the near future, the best scientific engineers will soon do likewise. The federal Government should act as soon as possible to prevent such an exodus which would have long-term disastrous effects.
Mr. Speaker, the Government should put an end to its cutbacks and encourage our young scientists to stay in this country.

subtopic: CALL FOR REACTIVATION OF ARCTIC AIRPORTS PROGRAM
CALL FOR REACTIVATION OF ARCTIC AIRPORTS PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, despite recommendations of the House of Commons Standing Committee on Transport, the Canadian Aviation Safety Board, and many others, the Arctic Airports Program still remains in limbo. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is on record as acknowledging the need for proper airstrips in remote areas, both for safety and economic reasons. Manicouagan has already been the beneficiary of his vision. However, about 11 identified locations exist in the Territories
where airstrips are either rudimentary and unsafe, or nonexistent. The Arctic Airports Program, which was allowed to expire by the previous Government, must be reactivated if northerners are to travel in safety.

subtopic: LETTING OF CLEANING CONTRACTS-EFFECT ON EMPLOYEES
LETTING OF CLEANING CONTRACTS-EFFECT ON EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada Post in letting out its new contracts for cleaning has robbed the lowest paid workers of their collectively negotiated rights by asking them to take a 50 per cent pay cut. Canada Post is taking advantage of the fact that labour law does not protect those people and their collectively negotiated settlement.
I call upon the Minister to meet with the workers in order to resolve this conflict and prevent a further deterioration in labour-management relations at Canada Post, which could threaten postal service in our country. Will the Minister take some action so that Canada Post cannot take advantage of the lowest paid workers who are being asked to take a 50 per cent wage cut?

subtopic: IMPORTANCE OF FIGHT AGAINST DRUG ABUSE
IMPORTANCE OF FIGHT AGAINST DRUG ABUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the recent report by the CUM Public Security Commission states that the fight against drug trafficking must be supported by political will.
I am proud that this Conservative Government already has recognized this and taken the steps needed. The Solicitor General has stressed once more his determination to set up a national strategy to reduce both the demand and supply of drugs.
Drug consumption is a problem that goes far beyond criminal acts and health hazards. Too often, it opens the door to criminal habits such as stealing, receiving, and sometimes even prostitution, all of which arise out of the need for drugs. The problem however is not exclusively a criminal one. It is an educational and a social problem. This is why the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) are joining efforts to find a solution. This is a national problem that requires a concerted effort on the part of all Canadian. This Government is doing its share, and all Canadian men and women should welcome this.

maintopic: INCREASE IN PRICE OF GASOLINE DECREED BY ULTRAMAR
INCREASE IN PRICE OF GASOLINE DECREED BY ULTRAMAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there were bad news for Quebecers today. The Ultramar Corporation has announced an increase of close to 2 cents a litre on gasoline at the pump.
Mr. Speaker, we all remember that nine months ago, this Conservative Government approved the purchase by Ultramar of the Gulf refinery and other facilities, so that it could shut down the Montreal East End refinery, reduce competition, secure a monopolistic position and increase fuel prices at the pump.
It is my hope that this Conservative Government and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) will ask Petro-Canada not to follow the bad example set up by Ultramar. And I am inviting all Quebecers to boycott Ultramar and to fill up at other stations where they can have cheaper gasoline.

subtopic: IMPORTANCE OF WEEKLY NEWSPAPERS-NECESSITY TO RETAIN SPECIAL POSTAL RATES
IMPORTANCE OF WEEKLY NEWSPAPERS-NECESSITY TO RETAIN SPECIAL POSTAL RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the first newspaper which I ever read was a community weekly newspaper. Like many Canadians, I continue to read such newspapers literally from cover to cover. For many of us who either grew up in rural communities or continue to live in rural communities, the weekly newspaper was and still is an important and sometimes the only source of information. Moreover, the weekly newspaper was and is a unifying factor, a source of local pride, and the personification of the community itself.
Due to the vastness of Canada, and the degree of isolation which exists in many of our rural communities, Governments historically have recognized the need to subsidize postal rates for many of our special interest publications, including weekly community newspapers.
Unfortunately Canada Post officials are now threatening to absolish those special postal rates. The end result, tragically, would be the demise of some local newspapers due to an insufficient number of subscribers and advertisers.
In light of the historic and continuing role of weeklies as community builders and supporters, I urge Canada Post officials and the Minister responsible to continue the policy of concessionary rates to this industry.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member suggested it was easy for a 10-year old child to come forward and take the stand in court, before a jury of 12 people. I would like him to amplify his point, because when I was sitting on the Badgley Commission, we heard several representations indicating that a child 10-year old or younger felt very nervous in the presence of a jury.
The groups that presented submissions really insisted that, in order for a child to be able to give evidence, the evidence should be taken as true, and no jury should be there. Otherwise the child will be frightened.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE AND CANADA EVIDENCE ACT
speechtext:
I thank the Hon. Member for her question, which is relevant. Clearly, an 8-or-10-year old cannot have the self-assurance of an adult before a court of justice. It is quite a
shock for any person to appear as a witness before a court of justice.
But this should be balanced against the right of the accused to be tried before a jury. And if the accused were to be deprived of that basic right, this would greatly prejudice any Canadian who is facing a serious charge.
But, I must say, in the light of my personal experience before the courts, that there are alternatives for a judge presiding in a case before a jury, like hearing witnesses in camera for instance. He may reduce the court staff. He may allow a child's mother or father to be in attendance during the testimony, and above all there is now a provision in this Bill that would allow the judge to ask that the accused himself be excluded. So who would remain in the court? The judge, perhaps a stenographer or a clerk. There would remain counsel for each side and 12 members of the jury, and this is much less frightening than what we now have considering that usually the courtrooms are generally filled with people.
This means that those new facilities made avaible to the courts by this legislation are reassuring in my view as to child testimony.
And may I add that, to my knowledge, the Badgley Report did not deal with 8-, 9-, or 10-year old children, because they are not the ones generally who are severely shocked, but rather teenagers aged 15, 16 and 17 who will have to tell of a sexual experience for instance, something they are not used to. So they are reluctant to tell about it. Whether there is a jury or not, I do not think this will change anything. And this is where understanding is needed from the judges, the counsels and everyone for that matter.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE AND CANADA EVIDENCE ACT
speechtext: I would like some further clarification. When the Hon. Member says that a child can suffer some trauma or more trauma than he would otherwise if he is 10 years old, does he mean that the child can be more or less intimidated? From his own experience, can a child be more or less traumatized depending on his age? Also, the Hon. Member emphasized the need for the accused to be there to defend himself, but we must remember that, in the case of sexual assault, the accused is often a relative. In most cases, it is the father, the stepfather, an uncle or other relative. I come back to my question. In that case, why did the Government not accept the recommendation of most of those who made submissions to the Badgley Commission, that is that children should be able to give evidence in a different atmosphere, without having the accused and the jury present?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE AND CANADA EVIDENCE ACT
speechtext:
There are two ways of making a charge. It can be done either by summary procedure, without a jury, or by indictment, which generally gives the accused the right to a trial by jury. The prosecutor, with the police officers who have prepared the charge, and probably the parents in this case since the rights of the victims must be protected and the parents are entitled to be present at such preliminary proceedings, decide together what type of procedure is appropriate in that particular case. This partly replies to the question.
November 4, 1986

However, if after this preliminary work, because of the seriousness of the charge, it is decided to proceed by indictment, in the case of an offence punishable by 14 years of imprisonment, for instance, if it is decided to bring a serious charge which can result in a serious sanction or sentence, I do not think that we can forget the rights of the accused, as he is facing a rather serious interference with his freedom. He is told that he could lose 14 years of freedom. I do not see how the accused in such a case could lose such a basic right as that of being judged by his peers, that is to a trial by jury.
I think that this Bill allows some flexibility. For certain charges, probably the majority, I imagine that the accused will be charged by summary procedure. He will therefore be facing a judge without a jury.
In very serious cases, when the freedom of an individual accused of a serious offense is involved, it will be possible to have a trial by jury, but there are other provisions which allow a judge to decide to exclude the accused from the court room when the witness gives evidence. This goes a long way toward protecting the child. I am personally convinced that this measure will have excellent results.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this new Bill, Bill C-15, is basically to protect children against sexual abuse and exploitation. Following a study of the Badgley Report, it was felt that amendments were needed to deal with sexual offences against children.
The amendments being proposed to provide increased protection for children may be summarized as follows: provisions for receiving unsworn evidence from children who are victims of sexual offences, without the need for corroboration; permission to videotape statements by a person under the age of eighteen in which he describes the acts complained of (the tape being admissible as evidence); provisions imposing severe sentences on persons who seek the sexual services of persons under the age of eighteen (up to five years imprisonment); provisions that raise the term of imprisonment from ten to fourteen years for those who live on the avails of prostitution of young persons under the age of eighteen.

November 4, 1986
Criminal Code
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the amendments provided in Bill C-15 will give children more effective protection against sexual abuse. In fact, this Bill draws heavily from recommendations contained in the Badgley Report, published in August 1984. I shall now give a more detailed assessment of some of the legal provisions included in this Bill.
I agree with Section 139 which provides that consent is no defence when the complainant is under fourteen. The fact is that even behaviour that does not resort to force or to the threat of such force or to misrepresentation or the exercise of authority can still be such as to unduly persuade a person under the age of eighteen to consent to the commission of a sexual offence, whatever it may be. In fact, the provisions of the new Section 139 are a direct reflection of Recommendation 13 of the Badgley Report.
As for the new sub-section 139(2) which provides that: "it is not a defence that the complainant consented to the activity that forms the subject-matter of the charge unless the accused (a) is aged twelve or thirteen years; (b) is less than three years older than the complainant; and (c) is neither in a position of trust or authority towards the complainant nor is a person with whom the complainant is in a relationship of dependency." I am somewhat puzzled, because it has been proven that young victims are as likely to be exposed to threats of force on the part of persons whose age is relatively close to theirs as they are to threats by those who are older, as far as participating in sexual acts is concerned. Assuming that the complainant is thirteen, the accused could be fifteen and thus avail himself of the provisions included in subsection 139(2). I would suggest that a 15-year-old adolescent is stronger than a 13-year-old adolescent and can therefore handle his younger brother and take advantage of him for sexual purposes.
Concerning clause 140 on sexual interference, I would like to see it amended along the lines of Badgley report recommendation No. 7 which reads as follows:
"Every person who, for sexual purposes, touches the genital or anal region of a young person with any part of the body or with any object is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to: (i) imprisonment for a term not exceeding 14 years if the complainant is under age 14, or (ii) imprisonment for 10 years if the complainant is between ages 14 and 16.
In this section, "young person" means a person under age 16.
The fact that the young person may have agreed to the activity which is the object of the charge, or that the accused may have thought the young person to be 16 years of age or older does not constitute a defence to a charge."
Again I would like new clause 154 on buggery to be amended along the lines of Badgley report recommendation No. 5 which reads as follows:
"Every male person who commits buggery on a female person who is not his wife and who is under age 18, or on a male person under age 18, is guilty of an indictable offence
and liable to: (i) imprisonment for a term not exceeding 14 years, if the person with whom the act was committed is under age 14; or (ii) imprisonment for five years if the person with whom the act was committed is between the ages of 14 and 18."
Similarly, new clause 155 on bestiality should be amended to take into account the Badgley report recommendation.
As to clauses 166 and 167 respectively, first the parent or guardian procuring sexual activity, and second the householder permitting sexual activity, I think the new text of law is appropriate.
In my judgment, however, the provisions concerning exposure and contained in section 169 should read as follows: "Every person who, for a sexual purpose, exposes his genital organs to a young person, is guilty of an offence punishable on summary declaration of guilt; in this section, "young person" means a person who is or, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, appears to be under the age of 16."
I agree with new section 195 concerning juvenile prostitution. The wording of subsections (2), (3) and (4) would seem adequate to protect children against this terrible scourge of our society.
As for the section which does away with the need for corroboration of a child's evidence, I agree with the provision that such corroboration is not necessary in order to convict a person accused of a sexual offence against a child.
I would like to see Recommendation 19 of the Badgley Report fully reflected in this Bill, because I think this particular recommendation was overlooked.
Finally, my concluding remarks concern the evidence of children who have been victims of a sexual offence. The new Bill remains silent in this respect. I feel that fundamental changes must be made in the legislation to enable children to testify on their own behalf in the course of judicial proceedings.
Although the testimony of victims of sexual offences is now considered with less scepticism than it was previously, the legislation is still very wary about evidence given by children. I think there should be no special provisions in this respect. The evidence given by a child should be heard and considered in the same way as that given by an adult. According to studies made for the Badgley Report, there is a very little basis in fact for assumptions that question the truthfulness of evidence given by children and their ability to clearly remember the facts of a sexual offence.
We can therefore say that young children are not more inclined to give vague descriptions to the police than are older children.
Consequently, I would like to see Recommendation 18 of the Badgley Report made part of the new Bill.
Finally, I would like to express my approval of a new provision in the Bill authorizing the presiding judge to exclude
November 4, 1986

the accused from the courtroom during the testimony of the complainant, if he is of the opinion that exclusion is necessary to obtain a full and candid account of the acts complained of from the complainant.
On the whole, I must admit this is a satisfactory Bill, but there are still many amendments to be made to the legislation, and I hope to have the opportunity of debating these amendments in committee. I also hope that enough time will be allowed for persons or groups wishing to make representations before the committee, so that everyone will be able to contribute.
I can assure you I will be taking an active part in the proceedings of this committee, but I still think a great deal remains to be done.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE AND CANADA EVIDENCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the serious problem of sexually abused children, the Government has now introduced in second reading Bill C-15, an Act to amend both the Criminal Code and the Canada Evidence Act.
The new provisions contained in this Bill will provide better protection for children because they will give more flexibility and strength to our legal system.
Obviously, the changes in the present legislation will have immediate effects on health and welfare programs. First, the new legislation will allow the authorities to institute proceedings against a greater number of offenders, and it is virtually certain that this will result in a greater number of charges and convictions.
Mr. Speaker, these offenders, and there have already been references to the Badgley Report and other studies on this subject, are nearly always men. Often, they are also the fathers, brothers or uncles of their young victims, and this constitutes a challenge to the legislators, as well as to the professionals, psychologists, psychiatrists, social workers, and all the others who must prepare the families to face the legal process and live with the consequences.
Also, the fact that these children will be able to give evidence before the court either on videotape or in person, will require special training for those who are in charge of these interviews so that they can carry them out not only in a way that will be legally acceptable, but also to avoid any psychological trauma for the child.
The judicial system as well as the social and health systems will have therefore to work hand in hand, not only in the particular cases which I have just mentioned, but also in other cases which I should like to review quickly.
Criminal Code
As everybody certainly knows, it is with a pluridisciplinary outlook that the Government announced on June 10 last a series of initiatives which was to include not only this bill under review, but also a major package of social legislation. From that moment, Hon. Jake Epp was designated as responsible Minister and undertook to set up in his Department a secretariat to coordinate all federal measures in his own Department and in all other departments concerned.
An interdepartmental committee has just been established to promote this coordination. This committee is made up of representatives from the Secretary of State, the Departments of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, of the Solicitor General, of Justice, of National Defence, and Status of Women Canada.
This new Secretariat will complete a wide range of programs already implemented by the Department of National Health and Welfare since 1978, including mainly a National Information Centre on Family Violence and the funding of numerous research and demonstration projects.
Mr. Speaker, all these years of work in the area of child abuse have given the Department a working experience and a global perspective on this issue, a perspective which places the current legal reforms in a quite unique social context.
Like any social or medical problem that arises suddenly and unexpectedly, sexual abuse has left us helpless as a modern society. Helpless first because the fact, as reported in the Badgley Report in 1984, that in a major survey, 50 per cent of women and 40 per cent of men did recognize that they had experienced undesired sexual acts before age 16.
Those who answered were people of all ages, that is 30-4060-year olds who remembered their childhood in the 1920's and 1930's.
In that half or so of Canadian men and women, there are still people who have been severely shocked and to-day they are the parents, the offenders or the teachers perhaps of our children.
For one reason or another, a large number of those people need help either themselves to be good parents, or because they are subject to persistent personal anxiety or to dangerous and hard to control behaviours.
Given that tragic problem, let me refer briefly to the approach and the measures that will be considered by the department over the next five years.
As you already know, $20 million have been earmarked for a program to help prevent and solve that problem. We must look at the issue, in a comprehensive and multidisciplinary way, about which do I need to stress, experts consistently agree. As in any family violence problem, whether children or battered wives are involved, the question must be addressed by all professions and at every level of society. In other words, it is not for governments alone to deal with sexual abuse. Professional associations, national non-government groups, school

November 4, 1986
Criminal Code
systems, benevole societies, people in general, everyone in both the private and public sectors has a specific role to play.
In almost all cases, the youth protection service remains the co-ordinating agency; sometimes task forces in hospitals play that role, that is they invite to a common table physicians, police officers, teachers and all sorts of experts to draw up guidelines to ensure a responsible and co-ordinated intervention.
One could ask what is the use of passing legislation to control criminal behaviour if the victims go unnoticed by the experts, if these experts have not learned to work with the police to set up well-documented files, if there is a lack of coordination between child welfare services, family courts and criminal courts before all of which the family has to appear?
The department will seek the co-operation of all sectors and disciplines. In its working context, Mr. Speaker, the department will have to always remain aware of the fact that the provinces are to be the first to intervene in cases of sexual abuses and provide with necessary follow-up services for the victims, the families, and the offenders. However, the federal Government has an important contribution to make by supporting the provinces in this work. The department is very much aware that all parties involved with the problems are overwhelmed by the frightening number of former and recent victims who report to the authorities day after day. It is essential to find long-term and short-term solutions which are both inexpensive and effective.
One solution of particular interest to the Department is to support systems whose contribution has not always been readily recognized and ask them to join in the task of educating the public and protecting and following up problem cases. I am thinking, for instance, of the churches which have played a supportive role for families, especially in rural areas. The job environment is also an excellent way to reach a large number of parents and make them aware of the issue of child abuse, while at the same time we could also increase their awareness of violence generally in the family.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a few minutes to consider the family context and the problem of violence in the home. Preliminary research has pointed out that abuse is often related to other problems existing in the family. For instance, a s.tudy in Alberta supports the results of research carried out in the United States which show that children who followed their mother to a shelter after the mother was abused by the husband or partner, were far more likely to suffer sexual abuse than children in the general population.
Studies have also shown there is a cycle of violence that goes on from generation to generation. In other words, girls who have been sexually or otherwise abused as children are more likely to become victims of abuse once they are adults, while boys who suffered sexual abuse are likely to repeat their experience by acting as the aggressor once they have become teenagers or adults.
The important thing to remember is that the problem of sexual abuse must be considered within the perspective of the family. This brings us to another very important aspect, namely, prevention. Considering the so-called cycle of violence, it is imperative to start prevention programs in order to persuade the general public to reject value systems that promote violence and sexual exploitation in particular.
Our knowledge of the way the public can be educated is still very basic, and much remains to be done to find out how we can inculcate more acceptable values. Long-term prevention is probably the best way to eradicate the problems of sexual abuse.
Mr. Speaker, we may be overwhelmed by the increasing number of cases being reported to provincial offices and police stations, and by the continuing shortage of services from agencies that are already working to full capacity, but it is also a fact that although the problem has been recognized, science has not yet had time to collect, examine and verify its various working assumptions.
We still have a long way to go before ascertaining which types of treatment are successful and which are ineffective. Were surgical science at the same point as sexual abuse is now, few of us would agree to an intervention. And still, given the numerous descriptions of recent and past victims, social and mental services must overcome uncertainties and help victims. Therefore the federal Government will fund research and demonstration projects to establish a sound basis for the treatment of victims and assailants alike. All the initiatives I have just mentioned will help professional staff deal directly with families and will have to be taken after consultation with experts in the field and the provincial Governments which are responsible for looking after the people involved, in a multidiscipline perspective.
To ensure success the Department is preparing a consultation for next fall to promote a concerted approach aimed at a national strategy in which all parties involved will participate, including the private and public sectors as well as the victims themselves. All Government levels will be represented: the federal Government, provincial and territorial administrations, municipalities and small communities. The preparatory work done this year and the results of next fall's meeting will be the basis of the program for the next four years. Without the participation of major Canadian institutions we would not even consider setting up prevention, research and general education programs, or preparing professional staff and the public at large to come to grips with this urgent problem. Mr. Speaker, we are seeking a national commitment.

Are there any questions or comments? There being none, I will recognize the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell).
November 4, 1986

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE AND CANADA EVIDENCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise to speak generally in support of Bill C-15, an Act to amend the Criminal Code and the Canada Evidence Act, which deals particularly with the very serious issue of child abuse. We support this Bill in principle. We are pleased that the Government brought it forward separately from other sections of the Bill which was presented in the last Session of Parliament. We had serious concerns about many of the sections dealing with pornography in that Bill. Although we want some amendments to this Bill, we support it generally in principle.
The portions of this Bill concerning juvenile prostitution and sexual abuse of children are of deep concern to me and my constituents, as I know they are to all members of the House. In Vancouver East we have had and still have very many young people on the streets involved in juvenile prostitution who were victims of sexual abuse as young children. I will speak about that a little later.
It is a great tragedy that the lives of so many young people are being ruined as a result of early sexual abuse. Unless there is some kind of treatment or intervention, very often their lives continue to be disfunctional in many ways as they become adults. My colleagues and I spoke very strongly in the debate on Bill C-49 on the need for stricter sanctions against the customers of juvenile prostitutes. I am pleased that there are some tougher sanctions applying to that contained in this Bill. This is, of course, only one aspect of dealing with the issue of juvenile prostitution. We need a multifaceted approach to dealing with young people on the streets.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), very ably analysed the concerns which we have about this Bill from a legislative point of view in his remarks this morning. I hope these matters can be improved through amendments. These are also concerns of the Canadian Council on Children and Youth. I refer Members to its analysis which is based on research and refers to concerns of the Badgely and Fraser Reports as well.
I would like to briefly summarize these concerns. First, under this Act a judge would be given the power to determine whether a child is capable of giving evidence. We find this to be far too subjective. I do not think it is fair to put judges in this position either. We believe that attention must be given to that section of the Bill. Second, there is the problem of whether the accused should be in court while a child is giving testimony. This Bill says that the accused may be in court. Surely this is a very intimidating experience for a young child who is being asked to testify against the person who has abused, frightened and damaged him or her and who may be sitting very close by in the court room. We do not feel that this is appropriate. It should not be allowed.
Third, we approve of the use of videotapes for taking evidence from a child. However, we do not feel there should be any time limit on this. I am sure that provision can be amended. It is obvious that we cannot just sit a child down and say that we are now going to talk about this terrible thing which
Criminal Code
happened. A child must have time to disclose information which is very painful and may be repressed. They must be in a very comfortable situation with people whom they trust. It is much better to do this at the appropriate time. I do not see why information obtained later should not be included on videotapes as well. It is certainly a better way of obtaining the information than in a very painful, formal and frightening situation.
Fourth, we are happy that the Bill does not require corroboration of a child's evidence. I have a very interesting article by June Callwood to which I refer members. She quotes an authority which states that children at about the age of six are able to make mature judgments on many matters, are able to speak for themselves and should be allowed to do so. The article to which I refer was in The Globe and Mail in October.
This Bill discriminates on the basis of sexual orientation. We believe there should be a consistent age of consent for both men and women. I believe that is practical and reasonable. This was recommended by the Special Committee on Equality Rights as well. Finally, it is quite unreasonable that the penalties prescribed in the Bill for beastiality exceed those for abuse of a child by a person of trust. Surely that should be changed.
I do not want to go into greater depth on the legislative issues which my colleague covered so ably this morning. Rather, as the critic for social policy, I would like to concentrate on some of the social aspects and implications of child abuse and the need for a much broader approach than is presented in this Bill. I believe very strongly that this is an obligation of the federal Government as well as provincial Governments.
In my earlier remarks I said that my colleagues and I are very concerned that so many young people are homeless and on the streets. There are young people from all over Canada on the streets of my riding. It is a real tragedy, not only that these young people are homeless but that they are involved in prostitution and drug abuse and often other illegal pursuits such as breaking and entering and other activities which are destructive to themselves as well as society. The case histories of many of these young people frequently reveal that they have been abused as younger children, often by people in their family such as a relative or friend who is a trusted person. If the abuse continues, this is extremely destructive to the child's personality.
These are the children who are withdrawn and anxious in school and have very low self worth. Often their teachers do not go beyond these symptoms to recognize that there is a very serious underlying family problem. They do not try to get help for the child but they have an obligation, as we all do, to do something about it.
I have also heard of cases of children who have gone to a doctor suffering from physical abuse. I saw a case on television

November 4, 1986
Criminal Code
involving a child with anal bleeding for which the doctor prescribed a diet of bran. The fact that this was a symptom of serious child abuse was not recognized. Medical and other professionals are reluctant to recognize child abuse, just as they are reluctant to recognize family violence and the battering of women. They are reluctant to intervene in family situations because it still seems to be part of our training that we do not interfere. However, it is extremely important to the protection of a child that we recognize what may be happening and intervene in such situations.
Furthermore, social workers often have little training in this field. In Vancouver, for example, unfortunately the Department of Human Resources had to retire, or fire, a sexual abuse team which consisted of the most skilled specialists in this field. They were recognized right across Canada and this team was very important as a resource to help train social workers and school personnel. That team was eliminated. During this time of restraint the Government also fired child care workers who were required to work on a one-to-one basis with children who had been abused, had family problems, and needed much help to recover.
I want to return to my remarks concerning young people on the street. Many of them are involved in prostitution. I have here a very realistic and moving article entitled "Street Youth in Vancouver", which was written by a youth worker, David Dranchuk. He has worked with young people on the streets for the past six years and is employed by the Anglican Church of Canada. I want to read from this because I believe he gives a very eloquent account of his personal and hurtful experience of what is happening to young people and what little we are doing about it. He says that Vancouver is the runaway capital of Canada. Some of the children are as young as 12, but most are around 15 or 16. These children come from all over Canada. He goes on to say:
Most of the children I find on the streets have a history of running. Often they are from unstable home situations or have already been removed and made wards of a child protection authority. Very often there is a history of abuse-physical, emotional or sexual; especially sexual abuse.
When I take a closer look, I find that these children have a lot more in common. They tend to have a very poor self imagine; perhaps the result of abuse. Not surprisingly, they have a profound distrust of adults in authority. Many are emotionally disturbed and don't feel wanted or accepted. For acceptance, they will do almost anything.
This need for acceptance is very significant. Because the street community is a very accepting one, they gravitate to the streets.
He goes on to say:
Before too long, the young runaway learns an important axiom of street life. Nothing comes for nothing. You have to pay. And because they have no money, sex becomes the common token of exchange. This is particularly true of girls who have been sexually abused at home.
If this child is not diverted from the streets and its sordid activity, he or she becomes entrenched into street life. It is not a good life. It is self destructive. I sometimes call it death on the installment plan.
Drugs are a big part of street life.
Drugs help to numb the pain of living. Drug overdoses are common. Sometimes the overdose is fatal. What a senseless waste of a young life!
He goes to note that there are practically no services that are relevant or usable by these young people. They are unable to stay in foster homes and landlords will not rent to them. Therefore, they end up on the streets. Employers will not hire them so they turn to drug trafficking, shoplifting and various forms of break and entering, theft, and prostitution. Wherever they go they seem to get repeated confirmation of their own lack of personal worth.
I know that where there are young people on the streets in my riding, people in the neighbourhood tend to abuse them and do not want to have anything to do with these kids. They do not even want a youth centre in the area. It is a very sad situation.
Mr. Dranchuk went on to say that many services are needed. I would appeal to the Government, particularly the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) in co-operation with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), to ensure that there are funds available and special projects are developed that will provide some of these services. Mr. Dranchuk states that they need more street workers because there are only three street workers in Vancouver for literally hundreds of kids. They must be special people who, themselves, can live on the streets and be accepted by street people. He goes on to say:
Also needed is a Youth Services Centre open seven days a week until about three in the morning. Besides trained counsellors, such a Centre should have emergency food along with laundry and shower facilities.
There are only one or two training programs that supposedly help young people but usually are not relevant at all. Once the bureaucratic screening and selection procedure is completed, young people who might begin to be interested simply drop out. If they happen to be lucky enough to get a job or into a job-training program, they are usually paid minimum wage so they often end up back on the streets because they do not have enough to live on.
Mr. Dranchuk also states that another needed facility is a "safe house" where street kids can stay for up to three days. These are suggestions by people who have experience with what can be done. The important point is that there is no funding available to provide these specialized services now and I urge the Ministers who are directly involved in this area to give some attention not just to imposing penalties through the law which, of course, must be done as far as customers are concerned, but to provide an alternative for these young kids who are on the streets for a reason.
There is also a need for prevention. We hear much about programs that have been initiated in some schools that are helping children to be more aware of potentially unsavoury relationships. One program in particular teaches children to say no if there is sexual touching that is likely to lead to sexual abuse. This is a progressive approach and I think many parents who are very anxious also need such programs to learn how to deal with this problem in an educational, relaxed way so that they are not over-anxious and creating an unhealthy situation for their children.
November 4, 1986

The legitimate concerns about child abuse are certainly much more open as a result of many public programs dealing with it. However, I hope that this approach to more awareness does not lead to over anxiety and near hysteria. I believe that is happening in some areas. In British Columbia there have been incidents of child abuse by teachers. This has caused a general backlash against the whole profession of teaching, which is grossly unfair. I think it is also very unfortunate if good teachers, or care givers of any kind, cannot show the normal kind of warm affection and responses which are important to children and to the relationship between a child and an adult.
I believe we have to do positive things in both prevention and treatment as well as through the laws, such as in the Bill before us, and we must ensure there is not a great hysteria. In our hearings on child care we are finding that parents are very reluctant to hire male child care workers in daycare centres, for example, which is very unfortunate. This again is because of reports of perhaps just one or two situations where there has been some child abuse. It is very important that we have male child care givers in our centres because so many of the youngsters do not have other male adults in their home environment.
Finally, I would like to take a moment to refer to many women who have been victims of sexual abuse or other forms of family violence and who may be in transition houses. There have been studies which show that women who have been abused often marry wife batterers and their children in turn may suffer from family violence. I recommend to all Hon. Members, and to the Committee on Justice, that they review a film which we showed very recently called "Breaking Silence". It is available from Women in Focus, a group in my riding of Vancouver. This film very eloquently shows many examples of women who have been victims of abuse and the terrible trauma which still remains with them as adults, affecting their lives, and the great importance of treatment and prevention for both adults and children.
I say once again that I am pleased to support this Bill, along with my colleagues. We think there are amendments needed, as well as a whole program which will deal with children and young people who have been abused.

If there is a mandatory exclusion, how would the New Democratic Party handle a situation where a
Criminal Code
man or woman represented themselves rather than be represented by a lawyer?

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE AND CANADA EVIDENCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join with my colleagues today in the debate on Bill C-15 which deals with amendments to the Criminal Code with respect to sexual abuse of children. I am pleased to hear from my colleagues on all sides of the House that there is agreement about the importance of these legislative changes and. the fact that they have been long awaited throughout the land.
I would like to review the situation and some of the background of which I am aware. We know, of course, of the excellent work done by the Badgley Commission. Its report was released in 1984. Perhaps, on the Canadian scene, this was the first time that the myths of child sexual abuse had been exploded. Up to that time people had been afraid to talk about the subject. We are now aware that it has been going on for many years. It is something which happened in secret and there had not been a great deal of public discussion.
I recall the first time I really became aware of how widespread it was is when I lived in Campbell River in the early 1980s. A very courageous young woman, who had been the victim of sexual abuse herself, finally spoke out and started a self-help group in the community. At that time there was no funding. She would go to various service clubs and groups to raise a little money here and a little money there for a telephone service or answering line. I sat in on some of those discussions and was amazed at just how shocked people were to even think that these things were happening. In this case,

November 4, 1986
Criminal Code
the woman had been sexually abused by her father. We could not believe this existed in a quiet and pleasant town. We became very aware of the impact the number of incidents of abuse had on that particular woman's life. Since those days there have been many different stories and books published on the subject.
When the Badgley Report was released, we were shocked as well by the statistics it presented, that at some time during their lives one in two females and one in three males have been victims of one or more unwanted sexual acts, that four in five of these unwanted sexual acts had first been committed against these persons when they were children or youths, that three in five sexually abused children have been threatened or physically coerced by their assailants and that one in four assailants is a family member or a person in a position of trust. About half are friends or acquaintances and only about one in six is a stranger. I think it is very sad and shocking to us all to find those kinds of things going on in our society.
We are very aware, of course, that this has been happening for centuries and statistics show that it is most generally women who as children have been the victims of sexual abuse and have been afraid to speak out. There is an interesting anthology published in 1983 entitled "I Never Told Anyone". It is writings by women survivors of child sexual abuse. It is this kind of book, along with others, which has brought this issue to the fore and have enabled women who have been victimized to speak out. I would like to read from the Preface by Louise Thornton:
This collection of women's voices speaks out about what is seldom said, seldom told, seldom acknowledged-the sexual violation of children. It is about the silence of nights spent holding in screams, holding back tears, holding in one's very self. And it is about the stillness of days when all of a young girl's resources are used up in keeping the secret from everyone, sometimes even herself. The women in this anthology are breaking this silence. Whether by whispers or cries or shouts or screams, they will continue to shatter it with the power of their own voices, their own words.
There are some very moving stories in this anthology. I think what is important is that over the last few years there has been a recognition of how important it is to speak out, and now we are beginning to help our children understand that.
I saw a television documentary last week which I believe was entitled, A Violent Secret. It depicted a young girl about 11 or 12 years of age who had been subjected to some unwanted sexual advances in a small town. She kept the issue a secret for a long time. The program depicted how her behaviour had been affected in terms of her friends and family because she felt so demeaned. I know the type of experiences young people go through because they do not understand what has happened to them and how destructive these experiences can be to their self image. This particular story had a happy ending in that the young girl was finally able to tell her parents and the perpetrator of the crime was brought to trial.
A National Film Board film entitled, Feeling Yes, Feeling No, is being shown in schools across the country. It is important that we begin to educate our young people about child sexual abuse. It is important for them to know that they do not have to take it and that if something happens to them they must tell someone whom they trust.
The legislation before us today is an important weapon in the fight against child sexual abuse. It deals with the legal framework. Other Hon. Members have mentioned today that we recognize this is only part of what we need to do. The rest has to be done through educational programs and support programs in communities. I am pleased to see that the federal Government, primarily through the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), is initiating programs in this area, as well as the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) through his missing children initiatives.
Often there is a connection. Many of the children who go missing have often been victims of some type of unwanted sexual abuse in their early days. Obviously, all of these matters tie together. What the communities are asking for is a stronger legislative framework which will more clearly enunciate the crimes involved and send a clear message to members of society that we will not condone the sexual abuse of children under any circumstances. The legislation before us is an important part of that process. There will be other legislation coming forward in terms of amendments to the Criminal Code which will deal with child pornography.
In terms of this legislation, I wish to pay recognition to the tremendous work that groups in communities across the land have undertaken. In this regard I think of my own riding of Capilano and, in particular, a woman in my riding, Mrs. Olive Wyatt, who has been personally dedicated to this issue for years. For some time she has been visiting different community groups to raise the issue and to appeal to these organizations. She has worked with the churches and is personally involved with the stores in my area in terms of getting them to take child pornography off the shelves. She has been consistent and persistent in her efforts. It is as a result of the efforts of such women, and others across the country, who have helped to raise public conscience and outrage with respect to this issue that has resulted in the Badgley Report and the Fraser Report, as well as the legislation which is before us today.
As has been said earlier, this legislation deals with several different areas. It makes provision for some new offences. A problem which existed before was that offences were not comprehensive enough to deal with the real situation. Included in the legislation is the new offence of sexual interference, which is an important one. Once the legislation is enacted, it will be an offence to touch anyone under the age of 14 years for a sexual purpose with any part of the body or an object. Sexual purpose is defined as one directed to the sexual arousal or gratification of the individual initiating the activity. I am pleased to see that this offence will be applied equally to boys and girls, which is something the equality committee recommended.
November 4, 1986

The second offence with which I wish to deal is the offence of invitation to sexual touching. This will go a long way toward dealing with a problem that existed before and which could not be dealt with effectively in criminal law. It will now be an offence for a person to invite or urge a child under the age of 14 years to touch another person in a sexual way. Often when we are dealing with children six years of age and under we find that they have been urged or invited to partake in such activity. They do not know that what they are doing is wrong and that it will cause trauma to them. The person who is making the invitation is the perpetrator of the offence and should be dealt with in a harsh way by the law.
The third new offence of sexual exploitation will add sections to the Criminal Code to protect young persons between the ages of 14 and 18 years from sexual abuse committed by persons in positions of trust or authority. As I mentioned before, it is a sad reality that much of the sexual abuse of children is carried out by persons in positions of trust, that is, relatives, friends, people whom the children know and of whom they have no reason to be afraid. Yet in such circumstances an incident can occur.
This legislation will prohibit a person in a position of trust from touching a child between the ages of 14 and 18 for a sexual purpose or from inviting them to touch any part of their own bodies or another person's body for a sexual purpose. These new offences which form the core of the amendments will be successful in laying charges in a number of instances in which it has not before been possible.
In terms of the presentation of evidence, we have heard a great deal about the subject in the past. It is very difficult for children to go into a courtroom situation, something which has been designed for adults. They are already traumatized by the events which have occurred to them. We are introducing provisions which will allow for the videotaping of evidence soon after an event has occurred which can be used as evidence at trial. Corroboration of a child's evidence will not be required since, in many cases, that is just not possible.
In certain circumstances a child will be allowed to give evidence without the accused being present. It can be a very humiliating experience for a child to give evidence in front of the accused. We know that what has happened in the past is that someone has known about a situation of child sexual abuse and yet has been unwilling to bring the offender to trial because of the former provisions involving the child and the giving of evidence. In those cases the family sometimes did not want to go through with it. What we are now saying is that it is an obligation to do this because the person who has committed the offence should not be allowed to continue in the same manner. We have to bring them to court and to punish them.
Another area with which the legislation deals is the important area of child prostitution. A new offence is created, that is, to be a customer of juvenile prostitution under any circumstances. A much heavier sentence is provided. There are increased penalties with respect to living off the avails of prostitution when a juvenile, either male or female under the
Criminal Code
age of 18 years, is involved. Sentences of up to 14 years have been provided for in these circumstances.
We know the tragedy of child prostitution. We know that in many cases juveniles, the children involved in prostitution, have come from circumstances in which they were either sexually abused or were the victims of other types of abuse in their own homes and that they have a very low sense of selfesteem. They do not have the support systems of their own families or friends and often they take to prostitution because they have been offered some type of friendship by a pimp or by other people. They think that that is the answer. Of course we know that it is not. In the circumstances in which they find themselves, the potential for violence and disease is even worse.
We need the laws. As my colleagues have said, we need the programs as well in order that we may provide alternatives for young people who have entered into prostitution. We should provide safe homes and training programs so that these people have other opportunities beyond prostitution.
We know from the evidnece that quite often, young women and men go into prostitution because they think it is an easy way to earn money. If they have no training, they feel that they have no other way of making money. We would suggest in those circumstances that there be other training options and opportunities for these people to earn money so they are not left on the streets.
There is a great deal that needs to be done yet. Personally, I am very pleased to see the initiatives the Government is taking in this legislation and in other ways. For example, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has established the office of a special adviser on child sexual abuse. This office will provide a co-ordinating point and there will be an interdepartmental committee of senior officials from all Departments involved including Health and Welfare, Justice, Secretary of State, Solicitor General and Indian and Northern Affairs. This committee will help co-ordinate our approach.
Of course, it is not just the federal Government alone that can help in these circumstances. We need to work with the provinces and the territories, with community groups and with volunteer organizations that have an interest in these issues as well. We in the federal Government are taking the initiative and are providing this leadership role. Although we know we will not eradicate the problem, we will raise public consciousness through these kinds of initiatives. We will be able to deal with these offences, we will be able to provide options and opportunities for young people and children who have suffered abuse and we will be able to provide a better life for them.
I look forward to the discussion in committee where we will deal with some of the specific issues in the Bill. I look forward as well to early passage of this legislation so that its provisions may come into effect.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I appreciated the speech made by the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins). Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. colleague for his questions. As he knows, later in the Session we will be dealing with amendments to the Criminal Code dealing with pornography. The Bill which was previously before the House contained special clauses dealing with child pornography.
I am not an expert on this and I cannot honestly say what kind of linkage there is. There is the perception that there is a linkage between child pornography and potential incidents of sexual abuse of children. I have read reports that go one way and the other on that so I cannot comment categorically on the true linkage. In my own opinion, child pornography is heinous and we should take very strong measures to ensure that it is eradicated from the shelves of supermarkets and from video cassettes.
Child pornography is degrading. Earlier, we talked of some of the consequences of sexual abuse. In some instances, the sexual abuse may be unwanted fondling or kissing but even that is degrading to someone who does not want to be touched or offended in that manner. It is particularly important for women to build their independence because women have often been the victims of this kind of pornography and abuse. I think it is important that it is made very clear that we do not accept that, whether it is in video cassettes, in magazines or in actual life. We need laws that deal very sternly and effectively with all of that.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Hnatyshyn that Bill C-15, an Act to amend the Criminal Code and the Canada Evidence Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE AND CANADA EVIDENCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in part, I am happy to be able to participate in this debate. I am happy that there is all-party consent to move ahead with these very positive amendments contained in Bill C-15, but I must also point out that I am a little unhappy because most of the people who have chosen to speak on this issue in the House have been women. I know some of the men have spoken out. Certainly we have heard from a spokesman from each Party. It is unfortunate that in the main the parliamentary push tends to come from women to deal with issues such as child abuse, pornography, and issues which affect the fabric of family life.
I would like to return for a moment to some of the practical applications not only of this Bill but of the whole issue of prosecution in child abuse cases. I had the privilege of serving as a Member of the Ontario Legislature on the Social Development Committee, which produced two reports on child abuse. This Committee travelled to a number of communities across Ontario.
One thing that came out loud and clear in the course of those hearings on child abuse was that notwithstanding very positive changes in the Criminal Code, or any efforts that we might make as parliamentarians, until child abuse as an issue comes out of the closet, there will continue to be children who will be molested, and families who harbour the molestation of children. Certainly those children whose families have the courage to confront the aggressor through the criminal justice system more often than not are spurned and have an experience which frankly would lead people away from reporting.
On a couple of occasions when we as Members of the Ontario Legislature investigated, a well-meaning parent or relative who became aware of the situation of child abuse had convinced the child to come forward. In some cases the child was of an age where they were able to testify under the old rules. Yet, because of the court process and the extremely complicated and lengthy jurisprudence involved in following up a child abuse case, in many instances the abused child had to go into court and repeat over and over the allegations. In many cases an acquittal resulted simply because of the insufficiency of the laws and the insufficiency of the uncorroborated testimony.
Although a number of these changes will serve to encourage people to report and get to the root of the cause of child abuse, it is my fear that unless we as a society and as a Parliament
Criminal Code
start speaking out more strongly on issues like child abuse and are prepared to talk about them, not only in the context of Parliament, but also in the work that we do on a daily basis across the country, too many child abuse cases will remain closet cases.
There was a case in my community where an acquittal resulted simply because the current cumbersome criminal justice system does not serve our children well. There are some positive changes. Certainly one is in the announcement by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) where he talks about the possibility of having videotaped testimony. I recognize the inherent dangers that this might present in terms of civil liberties and being able to confront your accuser.
If you talk to experts in the field, for example people from the Toronto Sick Children's Hospital, which has a division specializing in investigating cases of child abuse from a medical and psychological point of view, they will tell you that it is extremely important when dealing with the evidence and the testimony of a child of a certain age to telescope the number of interviews, interventions, and the number of adults who are involved in questioning a child who has been potentially subjected to child abuse. With every subsequent interview and court appearance, the notion that that child somehow is guilty of the offence is reinforced.
This is something that the changes in the law will serve to modify. They are recognizing the fact that a child who is not over the age of 14 can provide testimony which is uncorroborated and that the onus is upon the defendant, not upon the child and the child's lawyer, to make sure that that child is not capable of providing witness in a courtroom.
There are some other issues which have to be addressed. The Government chose to tread rather lightly in light of having been burned in the last session of Parliament on some of the rather wide-ranging and unacceptable changes to the pornography law, and wisely decided to break up the issue dealing specifically with child abuse from the general over-all issue of pornography. But at the.same time there is an element in the question of pornography which deserves to be dealt with in very short order. That is the issue of child pornography. It falls into the same category as the type of Bill that we are looking at today. There will hardly be a parliamentarian in the House who says that they do not support a move which will get tougher with child abusers. It is accepted that all Members of Parliament welcome the changes and would prefer that they become part of the Criminal Code as quickly as possible so that these people who are perpetrating heinous acts on young children will be punished.
The same sense of disgust and urgency appears when we deal with the issue of child pornography. At this point there has been no specific legislation in the House dealing with a curb on child pornography. What we have seen and what the Government is going to have to take some of the blame for is the cut-back on border enforcement. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made a comment in the House today about the crisis epidemic in drug abuse. It is fine to talk about the

is a plus; that is a positive thing. There is a number of positive changes in this piece of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, if we really want a family policy, it is not enough simply to talk about changes to the Criminal Code, because such changes do not cost us anything. However, what would be useful in addition to these amendments, which are valid and which will have the support of everyone in the House in my opinion, would be to do something about pornography, for instance. We know that, because of the new cutbacks at the excise division offices, where the Government has reduced the number of employees, we are admitting to Canada a much greater volume of pornographic material, involving both adults and children.
I think that it is important for the Government to reassert that we should not only protect our children, but also do what we must to pay the cost, because it will cost something to give all children under the age of four the right to child care services in Canada. From birth to the age of four, all children should have access to child care provided either by the parents, by sitters at home or by other people.
A long time ago, it would probably have been heresy to believe that everyone in Canada had the right to a high-school or even a university education. This was not a given right in the 20s, 30s, 40s, 50s or 60s. Canadians did not have a given right to post-secondary education. They now have this right because, in Canada, equality is a precious gift.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the principle of equality must apply first and foremost to our young children. Anyone who has studied psychology knows that children are psychologically and developmentally affected the most deeply by what happens to them between birth and the age of three. These are the findings of psychologists who have carried out numerous studies on children.
If we forego the responsibility in the case of single parent families or families where both parents work outside the home and provide no assistance for child care, it is obvious that all children will not be treated equally.
Mr. Speaker, if we support this Bill, which deals directly with changes to the Criminal Code in cases of child abuse, we should also urge the Government to introduce in the House a comprehensive family policy which would deal not only with the criminals brought before the Courts, but also with a strategy to reinforce the examination of pornographic material from abroad.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) reminded us again today in the House of the drug problem which affects many young people and which leads a lot of them to prostitution, for instance, to support their drug habits. It is not good enough to speak against these things, and the Government should have also a policy which would make it possible to hire more personnel for border enforcement in order to prevent any pornographic material involving children from coming to this country, just as we stop drugs from entering this country.
Criminal Code
What we are doing here is good and does not cost anything.
I think it would be good for the Canadian people to be aware that the House is willing and ready, not only to amend the Criminal Code, but also to allocate funds to develop a family policy which would encompass such issues as day care centres, pornography, the family council, etc. Those are very significant issues for Canada, and I think that we are taking today a major step forward. However, if we do not want to take two steps backward, we will have to back our policies with a decision to provide funds for this project; failing which, those would remain empty promises which cost nothing.
