speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) is the last speaker for the NDP and he will be returning from his office shortly to take part in this debate. Perhaps in the meantime I could say a word or two on the Bill.
We need to see Bill C-15 as another major step in the modernization of our Criminal Code, which is now almost 100 years old. Our society has changed rather dramatically over the last 90 some years, so it is clearly time for a major restructuring of the Code. Members will remember Bill C-18 from the first session of this Parliament where we made dramatic changes to the drunk driving sections of the Criminal Code. As a result, the number of accidents and deaths on the highway dropped precipitously.
As well, in 1979, before your time, Mr. Speaker, the then Minister of Justice, now Senator Jacques Flynn, under the leadership of Prime Minister Joe Clark, started a process involving the renewal of our Criminal Code. The Law Reform Commission looked at the entire Criminal Code. Now, very likely this month, we will be tabling in the House a first draft of the new model Criminal Code which will deal with substantive sections. Later on there will be a proposal with respect to procedure in the Criminal Code. As Members know, a commission dealing with sentencing will shortly be reporting.
It is my hope, as chairman of the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General, that Parliament will come together either with the committee, a subcommittee or indeed a special committee to take up these three streams of criminal law reform and pull them together so that by the centenary of our existing Criminal Code, which I think is 1992, we will have passed and proclaimed a brand new and modern Criminal Code which will take us into the 21st century.
1 would like to first deal with the comments made by the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell). I do not know that she was speaking officially for the NDP, but there is a provision in the law which says an accused may be excluded from the court while the allegedly abused child is giving his or

November 4, 1986
Criminal Code
her evidence. That seems sensible. We all know there can be continuing intimidation by someone in a position of power and authority over a young child. Yet we do not want to forget the principle of criminal law which says that the accused has the right to be present in court and to hear his accusers and hear the evidence against him or her. The judge, under this Bill, will have the discretion to exclude the accused.
If I understand the NDP position, and I may not, they want the Code amended so that the accused shall be excluded when the evidence of the child is being given. I would very much argue against that in principle. I believe we should leave that decision to a judge. For example, assume the accused is defending him or herself. How would you physically handle that? If the Code says they "shall" be excluded, then they shall be excluded. It seems to me there has to be some discretionary power here and I hope the NDP will review its position on that point.
I am sure that most Members will appreciate that this Bill provides a two-pronged approach to dealing with the rather alarming incidents of child sexual abuse by creating three new offences to protect children from sexual abuse. At the same time it amends the Canada Evidence Act to enable more children to testify in court. The Badgley Commission reported an alarming incidence of child sexual abuse but I will not go into the figures which were placed on the record by my colleague from Capilano. Suffice it to say that it is a problem which is at least being reported.
I am not sure that there is any more sexual abuse today than there ever has been, but it may be that there is an increase as a result of family breakups. In any case, it is clearly acknowledged today that there is a vast number of young people who have been sexually abused. I guess the real tragedy is that it is often done by someone in a position of trust, whether it be a parent, uncle, aunt or other relative. Obviously we need speedy passage of this Bill so that our children, who we all agree represent the future of this country, can grow up to be strong, straight and normal human beings.
With respect to the three new criminal offences, they are sexual interference, sexual exploitation and invitation to sexual touching. This would ensure that children under 14 years of age are protected almost absolutely from all manner of sexual contact, while children up to the age of 18 years would be protected from sexual exploitation by anyone in a position of trust or authority or on whom the child is dependant. At the age of 18 the young person would have full sexual autonomy and no longer receive special protection. The offence of sexual interference would protect both boys and girls under 14 from all manner of sexual contact.
This new offence would cover a range of activities from fondling of the child's genitals to full acts of vaginal or anal intercourse. Children 14 to 18 years of age could consent, as they are able to now, to all forms of sexual activity not otherwise prohibited by law, an example being buggery. However, the same child would be protected from sexual
exploitation by a person in authority or in a position of trust or a person on whom the child is dependant.
I see that my friend, the Member for Kamloops-Shuswap, is now back in the House. Since I will have the opportunity to deal with this Bill for hours and hours at committee, I will now stand down in order that he might rise.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must thank my very good friend, the Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker), for allowing me the opportunity to make a few remarks on Bill C-15. As he has indicated, as a member of the committee he will have an opportunity to comment during the committee hearings as well as at third reading stage. I appreciate the opportunity which he has provided to me today.
This Bill is an Act to amend the Criminal Code and the Canada Evidence Act. It provides for amendments to the Criminal Code to protect young people from sexual abuse and exploitation. Parliament is taking a very important and long overdue step today which deals with the tragedy of child sexual abuse. I am sure that every Member of this House believes that it is a tragedy that such a growing number of young people in our country are caught up in this disastrous situation. ' As responsible Members of Parliament, we have an obligation to deal with child sexual abuse as quickly and effectively as possible as one step toward bringing an end to this very serious tragedy.
The tragedy associated with child sexual abuse was reported on extensively by the Badgely Committee. That report identified the present situation of child sexual abuse in Canada as a hidden tragedy. The report called it a hidden tragedy because for so many years its widespread nature was not well known or understood. It is now coming more and more into the public eye. I am told that in Kamloops approximately six or seven cases of child sexual abuse are reported to the authorities every week. Those are only the cases which are reported. I suspect that, as with so many other things, for every case which is reported there are many more which are unreported and remain part of this hidden tragedy. Of course, that is to say nothing of the hundreds of young boys and girls in my constituency of Kamloops-Shuswap who are in what social workers call "care", meaning that they have been forced to leave their normal homes and are being cared for in one context or another.
The Badgely Commission uncovered an almost unbelievable level of child sexual abuse and exploitation. It referred to the cyclical nature of child sexual abuse. That, of course, refers to the fact that those who abuse young people sexually today were themselves victims of child sexual abuse earlier in their
November 4, 1986

lives. The challenge is for us to do whatever is necessary to bring an end to this vicious and hideous cycle of child sexual abuse.
In its report the Badgely Commission suggested that we must strengthen the Criminal Code to deal more effectively with child sexual abuse. I am sure that all Members of Parliament are often visited in their constituency offices by parents, and particularly by mothers, who report a fear for the lives of their children. They are shocked by events which become public in their own neighbourhoods. The Members for Vancouver Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) and Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) have spoken of the tragedy of young people on the streets of so many Canadian cities who have fallen victim to sexual abuse and exploitation of one kind or another. In our constituency offices we are informed of individual tragedies and urged to do whatever we can to bring an end to this very serious situation.
We New Democrats will do everything possible to expedite the passage of this Bill in order to bring it into effect as quickly as possible. We regret, however, that we could have been dealing with this matter much earlier. The Badgely Commission tabled its report in August of 1984. It is only today, more than two years later, that the Government has decided to introduce Bill C-15 which attempts to implement through law a number of the recommendations of the Badgely Commission. Therefore, while we are pleased to be finally dealing with this, it is unfortunate that it was not dealt with much earlier.
As I said, we New Democrats are very serious about this matter and will do whatever we can to facilitate the early passage of this legislation. We have some concerns and would like to make some suggestions to make the Bill more effective. When the Bill is referred to the Justice Committee, we will certainly make a number of suggestions in that regard. We will call for a number of groups and organizations to appear as witnesses to provide suggestions as to how this legislation can be made more effective. We will also seek suggestions of other ways in which we might deal with child sexual abuse.
The Bill before us protects children from sexual touching. It protects young people from those who might take advantage of their position of authority, trust and dependency. I need not recount reports which have become public over the past number of months of people who have taken advantage, in a sexual way, of their positions of authority, trust or dependency. This tragedy is often hidden because it often involves parents, other people in the home, members of an extended family or close friends, which makes the situation all the more hideous.
As well, this legislation addresses the exploitation of children as prostitutes, both in terms of the users of child prostitutes and those living off the avails of child prostitution. This is a most serious situation. Young people who become part of the community known as street people in our cities are often forced to prostitute themselves on our streets because the existing facilities and agencies are unable to meet their needs.
Criminal Code
I am pleased that this legislation is a step toward dealing with those who exploit these tragic young people. Those who are living off the avails of prostitution will be dealt with in an especially harsh way. It is open to discussion whether the measures are harsh enough and such discussion will take place in committee. However, I cannot imagine that we could be too harsh on people who take advantage of the plight of young people and exploit them sexually. Of course, the problem in the past has often been the insufficient number of cases that actually get to court. This legislation attempts to give new definitions of what is to be considered unacceptable behaviour when it comes to child sexual abuse, and a new definition of persons in authority in an effort to more closely identify who they are.
The Bill also calls for the judge to utilize the information that is provided by young girls and boys. There is some concern that these young people need to be above average intelligence before the judge or jury can use the information and evidence that they provide. We have some concerns that this above average intelligence test case situation, by definition, would probably eliminate half the children. I suggest we should use children who are able to provide appropriate, adequate evidence, regardless of what we might think about their level of intelligence. 1 believe it would be relatively easy for a judge or jury to determine that intelligence.
I am pleased that the Bill includes the admission of videotape evidence taken shortly after the offence. My hon. colleague, the Member for Burnaby, has indicated that this could also include audiotape evidence, particularly in those areas where it is difficult to obtain videotape, such as rural areas. This is another matter that can be developed more thoroughly in committee.
Furthermore, the Bill provides an opportunity for the judge and jury to view the body language of the child as the child is providing evidence. Those of us who are parents often know that we can often tell more about our children by their body language and facial expressions than by what they are saying. Therefore, I believe videotape evidence will be a useful new approach.
It is possible for three to five years to pass from the time of the incident to a judge actually delivering a decision. Such an interval can cause problems, particularly when the videotape evidence was given shortly after the offence. We may want to take advantage of using that type of evidence after the young boy or girl has had an opportunity to deal with the tragic event in their own way and perhaps provide further evidence later.
I believe this is the first time it has been proposed to exclude the accused from the courtroom. Since a young boy or girl may feel intimidated if the accused person was before them in the courtroom when they were providing evidence, I believe this is a major step forward. However, there are a number of concerns which must be examined in the committee.

November 4, 1986
Criminal Code
While I am pleased that we are dealing with amendments to the Criminal Code dealing with child sexual abuse, it is important that we recognize that it is simply one small step toward eliminating child sexual abuse in Canada. There are a number of other federal, provincial, and local government initiatives that should be taken, particularly by providing the resources to assist in the counselling of victims of child sexual abuse. Too often there are not enough adequate resources to provide proper counselling to the hundreds of thousands of young people who are exposed to sexual exploitation. This aids and abets the child sexual abuse cycle to which I referred earlier, to say nothing about adults who seek counselling or legal means to deal with sexual abuse they experienced as children.
We should also recognize that the offenders who are involved must be treated. It is not appropriate to ignore people who have committed or been convicted of child sexual abuse, knowing full well it will be a matter of months or years before they are on the streets of Canada again. It is in the best interests of our society to deal with these offenders by treating them through proper counselling.
The existing programs must be better co-ordinated. The Hon. Member for Burnaby indicated that most provinces today do not recognize child sexual abuse as a definition of behaviour requiring child protection in provincial jurisdiction. Not only must this be changed, it is an example of so many problems that need co-ordination in order to maximize their effectiveness.
The case overload for those professionals dealing with child sexual abuse or violence associated with young people is becoming normal. I have many friends in my constituency who are social workers. They have described their caseloads to me and I cannot imagine how they can begin to deal effectively with any of the cases when they are so overworked and the demand on the system is so horrendous. If the Government is serious about dealing with the abuse of children, it should take the opportunity to provide the professionals and the support systems with resources to do the job that is required.
Let me point out to the House that in June, 1986, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) promised the people of Canada that he would appoint a special adviser to co-ordinate the Government's response to child sexual abuse. I remind the House, particularly members of the Cabinet who are here today, that five months have passed since that announcement. I cannot imagine a more welcome appointment, particularly with the introduction of this legislation, and I hope the Minister makes that announcement soon.
Let us examine the degree to which the Government is concerned about child sexual abuse. The Bill is a step in the right direction and we have heard some very thoughtful speeches in the House of Commons today. However, let us consider what the Government is spending to deal with child sexual abuse. It recently announced that it plans to spend $20 million over five years. That is probably what it spends in one
year for brandy and cigars during entertainment parties. The expenditure of $20 million over five years to combat child sexual abuse in Canada is simply inadequate and inappropriate. The Government can show its concern and commitment to deal effectively with eliminating child sexual abuse by providing the adequate resources and funds to ensure that the appropriate programs, agencies, organizations and individuals are mobilized to combat this tragedy.
In closing, I suggest we must carefully consider what we do as Members of Parliament. I want to refer to Section 43 of the Criminal Code which essentially legalizes violence against children, whether that is in the schools through corporal punishment or by spanking. It is legalized in our Criminal Code and I believe that when we are concerned about violence, violence against children in this case, we should recognize that we ought to remove that section from the Criminal Code.
We must also recognize the violence and abuse associated with poverty in our country. All Hon. Members have spoken about the increasing levels of poverty in Canada. We know that many children in our constituencies come from very poor families and we are aware of the abuse in their lives as a result of that poverty. We in the New Democratic Party will support this Bill in principle and will work to improve it.
I want to conclude by suggesting that if we are concerned about child sexual abuse, the exploitation of children, and violence against children in one form or another, we should take a second look at the kind of entertainment we provide through television and the kind of toys sold in our stores. The Rambo-style doll, the violence and killing shown on television and the violent games on the video machines young people involve themselves with, I suppose, makes it an extension of a young person's life to kill indirectly through television or the video screen perhaps thousands and thousands of people. They see it often glorified in the Rambo-style entertainment. That is something which is topic for another discussion, but in my opinion, when we talk about ways and means of ridding our country of child sexual abuse and violence, it is something we should keep in mind.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for offering to cooperate with the Government and indicating her party's intention to support this Bill. I think this goes along the line of the Badgley and Fraser Commission reports which were asking all Canadians, all political parties, all people interested in this matter to set aside all political bias and to move forward in the best interest of Canadian children. My hon. colleague's co-operation, therefore, is consistent with these views.
Now, I have listened attentively to her recommendations concerning Section 43 of the Criminal Code, and I suggest
November 4, 1986

they should be carefully looked into. For that matter, this Bill is based on a concept which is somewhat new, that is to say a relationship of trust and dependency to which we are not really accustomed in our legislation and which, I think, may provide a solution to many problems.
This dependency which is stated at the outset of this Bill and establishes quite clearly that when a person is in a situation of authority towards another, or when a child is in a relationship of dependency towards an adult or another person, such a person would be guilty of an indictable offence and liable to more severe penalties, and could not use as a defence the consent of the victimized child.
These new provisions, I think, are consistent with what my hon. colleague has suggested under Section 43, and I should like to hear her comments concerning this new concept of authority in the light of her suggestion about Section 43 of the Criminal Code.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the comments of the Hon. Member. I simply want to reiterate that since we are at second reading stage of the Bill and discussing its principle, I cannot express strongly enough how much my party and I support the principle of the Bill. It is long overdue. I wish we would have had the opportunity two years ago to debate this Bill with the new Government. I wish we would have had the opportunity to debate the Bill many years ago with the previous Government. However, we are debating it today and we appreciate that.
Protecting young people from those who might take advantage of them, those in positions of authority, trust and dependency, is a most appropriate part of the Bill. There have been many examples made public recently of people in positions of authority-I think they are well known and publicized so I will not refer to specific cases-and members of the family, fathers, uncles, and so on. Individuals who exploit special situations where people are dependent upon them must be dealt with severely. The Bill attempts to define more carefully what these positions are, and the definitions associated with them, in the hope of being able to deal more effectively in the courts with people who find themselves falling within the definition of "authority and trust".
It is important to recognize that when dealing with this very fundamental and basic question, some very startling figures come to mind. Ninety-eight per cent of people who use and abuse customers who are children, young boys and girls, are men. Men are the consumers, the customers and, unfortunately, they are pimps who are involved in the business associated with child sexual abuse. These people must be dealt with. We have to recognize that sexual responses in today's society are certainly by and large a learned behaviour, particularly in the kinds of situations with which we are dealing in this legislation. It is time that we as a society and as Members of Parliament do what we can to get away from this macho image
Criminal Code
of sexuality where the male is the dominant superior participant and deal with sex on a completely different basis, where there is no master, no superior participant. In the socialization of our society this is a clear model and is something we must all do what we can to eliminate and change.
To react directly to the points made by the Hon. Member, this is a very important piece of legislation and while we will co-operate and act as expeditiously as is reasonable, we feel it should receive debate and discussion. Quite frankly, I have heard some of the most valuable and thoughtful presentations today in the House from all sides. I think we have struck a chord. We are dealing with an issue, a tragedy, about which all of us feel very strongly and we are pleased to be making an effort today, at least as a first step, to remove and eliminate child sexual abuse in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I just have a very brief question in the spirit of co-operation. I am quite impressed with the quality of the speeches. I do think we have a message to give to the public and that is we indeed want their input. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to make a few comments with respect to Bill
C-15 which deals with amendments to the Criminal Code and amendments to the Canada Evidence Act. Specifically, it deals with the subject of child sexual abuse and exploitation.
I can tell Hon. Members that legislation of this type is welcome throughout the country. I know it will be welcomed by my constituents in Niagara Falls who applaud the Government and the House for moving forward with legislation in this area. One thing we should do with a law of this type is put it into context in terms of what we as a Government have tried to do with the Criminal Code. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker), has indicated that we are approaching the one-hundredth anniversary of the Criminal Code. It is certainly my opinion, and one shared by many of my colleagues in the Government and other Members of the House, that many revisions have been necessary to the Criminal Code. Some of them have been made already and, obviously, there will be more to come. I put those amendments in this context as well.
I believe that the provisions of this legislation fit in well with other moves taken by the Government which have tried to take better care and show more concern for the victims of crime. In terms of the legislation which is before us the victims, of course, are children. Other moves that we have taken have provided protection for all Canadians. This is a good and valid point, and something with which the House has had to deal. The Criminal Code, as well as the interpretation of it, has for too long and in too many instances been not enough concerned with victims' rights. This was made clear to me when the House was recalled during the summer to pass the legislation dealing with dangerous offenders.
After that legislation was passed, someone from the press said that there was criticism being expressed in the country that we are not concerned enough with the rehabilitation of criminals. I replied quite honestly. I said that the people who sent me from Niagara Falls to this House are law-abiding people. They are people who have something to say and who want to be protected by the Criminal Code. For too long and in too many cases their rights and concerns have not been expressed.
I can tell Hon. Members that I am proud to be a member of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. It has been a very active committee. I will not go so far as to say that it is the most active since someone may correct me on that point. However, I will say it is as active and as busy a committee as we have seen in the Thirty-third Parliament.
Our committee has dealt with a number of issues. Hon. Members will remember that shortly after our election a decision came down from the Supreme Court of Canada which struck down the Criminal Code provisions with respect to the importation of hard-core pornography. I was pleased that we did not wait two or three years to do something about that decision. We did not hum and haw and say that that is the way things go, that the garbage will now come across the border into our country. Within 10 days the then Solicitor General tabled legislation in the House making it illegal to import
November 4, 1986

hard-core pornography into the country. That is one example of the Government's worry about those who are exploited by hard-core pornography and how we protect the values which we as Canadians hold. What the Government has done is to move toward protecting in a more responsible way the victims of crime. The Speech from the Throne reiterated our commitment to family values. I believe this is something on which the people of Canada count. Our record with respect to justice matters bears that out.
We had the whole subject of prostitution and, in particular, street soliciting before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs in the form of Bill C-49. Those of my colleagues who sat with me on that committee and those who watched the debates in the House of Commons were told again and again by the critics of the Bill all the dire, terrible things that would happen. We were told that all we would have to do is wave at someone and we would find ourselves in jail. In fact, what has happened in the last few months since the Bill's passage is that we have seen a beneficial effect for a great number of people in the country. In my riding of Niagara Falls where this has been a particular problem, I have been told again and again by the merchants and by those who are responsible for enforcing the law that it is working. The situation has been controlled.
I was very interested to read a comment made by a woman who had been engaged in prostitution in the City of Ottawa. She said that the way things were going, she would have to get out of the business. There are many members of my party and I am sure of the other parties in the House who would welcome that. That is not the kind of profession in which we wish to see people. That move away from prostitution was one of the by-products of Bill C-49. We made the point very clearly in that legislation and we are making it in this legislation as well.
An interesting comment was made by an Hon. Member concerning the entire subject of sexual abuse and the role to be played by all of us in society. She mentioned specifically the early warning signs that can be seen by child care workers. It has been my privilege these last few months to be a member of the Special Committee on Child Care, a special committee very ably chaired by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Lincoln (Mrs. Martin), who has done an outstanding job in organizing and co-ordinating the Government's investigation into that subject. We heard that child care workers across the country are in a unique position to observe the effects of and to detect child abuse. It is so important to detect such a thing at that age because of the pernicious nature of child sexual abuse and the damage it can do to children. It is incumbent upon all of us to deal with this problem as early as possible. Many times, a child's first exposure to the outside world takes place in a daycare centre or a family child care centre.
Without prejudging what the committee will do, it was made clear to us that we must impress upon those who deal with children at a very early age the importance of recognizing
Criminal Code
the signs of child abuse. We as a society must encourage the detection of child abuse. People told us that they were afraid to speak up. Perhaps they suspected something was wrong but they were afraid to come forward. They thought that they might somehow be liable or subjects of reprisals. We as a society must encourage people again and again. We must tell them about the different signs for which they should look and remind them of their obligations to children and to Canadian society as a whole.
The fight against child sexual abuse is not confined only to daycare centres. The responsibility to do something about human exploitation rests on all of us as a society. In the last few years, how many of us have entered neighbourhood candy stores and video rental stores to see some of the hard-core pornography and kiddy porn that is on the shelves? I believe we have a responsibility to do something about this.
Simply expecting the Government to do something seems to be a Canadian disease. Everyone thinks that if there is a problem in Canada, Ottawa had better do something about it and spend money on it. However, I believe it is the responsibility of all of us. When we go into corner candy stores and see garbage on the shelves that is offensive to us and our children, we have the obligation to speak up and say that that is not the kind of thing we want to see on the shelves.
When I went to candy stores 25 years ago, comic books were being sold. I remember people saying that I should not be reading comic books because they were not good for me and would hurt my development in the English language, the one in which I was brought up. I think most parents would say now that if only comic books were in the corner candy stores, they could accept that. Now, however, many corner candy stores carry what is in my opinion hard-core pornography. I believe we must do something about that.
Earlier in this Session, I posed a question to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn). I told him that I, the people of Niagara Falls and many of my colleagues would welcome new legislation designed to deal with violent and hard-core pornography. I received an assurance from the Minister of Justice that something would be done and I welcomed that assurance just as I welcome this law.
There are many aspects to this law. I am particularly pleased that we will deal with the problems of sexual interference and invitation to sexual touching. The new Criminal Code provisions will make it an offence to touch anyone under the age of 14 for a sexual purpose. As well, the new legislation will make it an offence to invite or urge a child under 14 to touch another person in a sexual way. As several of my colleagues have pointed out, we have concluded that the age of sexual autonomy for most purposes will be the age of 18, and I believe that is valid. We as a society have an obligation to protect children under the age of 18 in the way outlined in this piece of legislation.
Among other things, this legislation deals with the problem of sexual exploitation and attempts to protect children under

November 4, 1986
Criminal Code
the age of 18 from that. A number of people have pointed out that this is a very serious problem. I believe it was the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) who said that it is a hidden crime and I must agree with him. For too long, this sort of thing has gone on.
I have referred to some of the bad things that have happened to Canadian society in terms of tolerance of pornography, but I can say that there is a growing awareness of the problems faced by children and other persons who are in a position to be exploited by persons in positions of trust. I will be very pleased to see that matter referred to the committee for discussion.
As well, this legislation deals with the subject of prostitution. It provides that a customer who seeks to obtain the sexual services of an individual under the age of 18 is liable to five years in prison. I believe that that is a tremendous provision. That is one of the reasons Bill C-49, the law on street soliciting, works. It goes after the customers as well. There is nothing that will clean up juvenile prostitution or prostitution in general quicker than to get at the customers. When the customers are afraid to get involved, it becomes possible for those who want to get out of this business to do so, to get on with their lives in a way I think most people would think proper.
I am pleased that those who live off the avails of juvenile prostitution, the pimps, have been dealt with in this legislation as well. The penalties for that crime have been increased from 10 years to 14 years imprisonment and that is good as well.
I see I have only a few moments left, Mr. Speaker. I would like to make some comments about changes to the Canada Evidence Act. One of the clauses in the Bill deals with the problems involved when children take oaths. This can be a frustrating and difficult part of a case involving child sexual abuse.
I was in court one day as counsel and was able to observe what happened with respect to a child who was accusing a young man of sexual abuse. I believe the child was eight or nine years old. As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, under the Canada Evidence Act, the judge has to make inquiries as to whether or not the complainant understands the nature and quality of an oath. In that particular case, the judge could have ruled either way. I do not think the child understood the oath in the traditional way, the way I was brought up to understand it.
If it is decided that a child does not understand an oath, the consequences are that the child's evidence must be corroborated. The combination of the two can be fatal. If the child does not understand the nature and quality of an oath and if there is no corroboration, there generally is no case. In most cases of child sexual abuse there are no witnesses. It is done in an alley or in someone's basement. It is done away from other people or witnesses. The changes are very good. I am encouraged to see that improvement.
I also notice that videotaped statements are now permitted where a child claims sexual abuse. That videotaped evidence is to be taken very soon after the complaint is made. One of the problems is that it becomes an excruciatingly difficult and trying time for the child who has made this accusation. They are questioned again and again. Mr. Speaker, you are aware of the legal process in this country. Generally, it is many months before a preliminary hearing. It may be a couple of years before the trial.
There are a number of things by which all of us can be very encouraged. The Government is to be commended. This is the type of legislation that Canadians want and deserve. It fits in with the other positive moves made in the Criminal Code. I welcome them. I would urge my colleagues to get this to the committee stage as quickly as possible, so that this very soon can become the law of the land.

speechtext:
I have listened with interest to the comments of my colleague from Niagara Falls (Mr. Nicholson) who is a member of the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General. subtopic: BANKRUPTCIES-SUPPLIERS' RIGHT TO REPOSSESS GOODS
BANKRUPTCIES-SUPPLIERS' RIGHT TO REPOSSESS GOODS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 15 I directed a question to the Minister of Consumer and

November 4, 1986
Adjournment Debate
Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) with respect to the Government's upcoming legislation on bankruptcy as it will pertain to suppliers' rights to repossess goods for which they were not paid. The Minister assured me that the Government would hopefully bring forward recommendations for change to the Bankruptcy Act in the near future.
As indeed most Members of the House are aware, there are many shortcomings in the existing bankruptcy legislation. I commend the Minister for addressing this matter which has been overlooked for too long. However, it is imperative that I indicate to the Minister the dangers of leaving unattended the inadequacies contained within the Bankruptcy Act, as they fail to pertain to the protection of the Canadian supplier and wage-earner. One has only to look around in Canadian society at the problems caused by the failure of the Act to protect the Canadian supplier and wage-earner.
As the Minister is well aware, Parliament passed the Bankruptcy Act in 1949. However, since then there have been increasing problems with the legislation. This is amply illustrated by the fact that there have been six unsuccessful attempts to change its provisions over the past few years.
Under current law no special consideration is given to suppliers in bankruptcy situations. For example, a supplier could deliver goods to a business on a Friday and the business could be closed or bankrupt by the Saturday, and the supplier is unprotected. Of course this points out a very grave shortcoming. I ask the Minister to consider a measure taken in Quebec some time ago giving the suppliers of bankrupt businesses 30 days after the appointment of a trustee in bankruptcy in which to repossess goods for which they had not been paid.
As well, wage-earners have received the short end of the stick in bankruptcy legislation for far too long. It is time that wage-earners be suitably protected with new bankruptcy laws up to a limit of $2,000. They should be given priority to secured creditors, namely, banks, Crown corporations and Crown agencies. These men and women have rightfully earned the wages and rely upon them as their sole means of sustenance.
The matter has been neglected far too long. It is not only wage-earners, but those persons employed on a commission basis in the area of sales. Sales commissions and expenses should also be considered in the same manner as wages. Salesmen who were on the road and incurred expenses can be left high and dry under the current law.
Once again I urge the Minister to reconsider changing the Bankruptcy Act and to ensure that suppliers of goods, wage-earners, and sales people on commission receive priority treatment ahead of secured creditors such as banks, Crown corporations, Crown agencies, Revenue Canada, sales tax departments, and so on. It is long overdue. These people should get what is rightfully theirs.
Again I commend the Minister on his initiative, but I also say to him that it is time to redress a grave injustice to many Canadians.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: BANKRUPTCIES-SUPPLIERS' RIGHT TO REPOSSESS GOODS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to provide additional information to the answer given by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) to a question put on October 15, 1986 by the Hon. Member for London East (Mr. Jepson). That question dealt with the status of suppliers of goods in the proposed amendments to the Bankruptcy Act. The Hon. Member was hoping that provisions would be introduced to allow an unpaid supplier to repossess the goods delivered to an insolvent debtor. He was referring to the system in effect in Quebec, under which suppliers of goods enjoy that right in that province.
As indicated by the Minister, the issue of unpaid suppliers is now under consideration by him. I must stress however that a decision has been made to review the Bankruptcy Act by stages.
Over the past 16 years, 6 attempts at completely remodelling the Bankruptcy Act have failed. For that reason, a list of questions to be dealt with has been compiled, and it has been decided that the most urgent would be adressed as a priority. The five issues identified as having top priority are: the protection of wage earners; provisions with respect to the activities of secured creditors and receivers; provisions to promote financial reorganizations; provisions dealing with bankruptcies and consumer offers; and, finally, the Crown's preference as a creditor. At the same time, a number of amendments of a rather technical nature, aimed at improving the efficiency of the bankruptcy system, will be tabled.
Although the importance of the problem of suppliers of goods is fully recognized, the aforementioned issues have been identified as the most urgent and ready to be solved. On the other hand, I am in a position to assure the House that the Minister intends to address the matter of suppliers in a later stage of that review.
The matter of unpaid suppliers is still under consideration. Incidentally, the possibility of using a system similar to that in Quebec has been considered, but as yet no decision has been made.
I think it would be useful to clarify the extent to which unpaid suppliers enjoy a right to repossess under the Quebec Civil Code. The Hon. Member should be aware that this right in Quebec applies only under certain conditions, namely that the goods delivered have not been sold to a third party, that those goods were in the same condition as when sold, and only if the request for repossession is made within 30 days following delivery of the goods.
November 4, 1986

Earlier this year, the Government passed a law to help farmers experiencing financial difficulty. I am of course referring to the Farm Debt Review Act. This was the first element of a series of measures intended to improve federal bankruptcy legislation.
Hopefully, the Government will be able to introduce the next, and second element soon. That would be the package of amendments I referred to earlier. Following that, it is intended that additional outstanding issues, including the status of unpaid suppliers, be addressed as expeditiously as possible.

speechtext:
This
evening, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to a question I directed to the Minister responsible for Canada Post last October 28. We had just learned that Canada Post had prepared a communication plan, a rather thick document, in an attempt to manipulate Canadians and sell them on the forthcoming postal rate increase.
A few days later, Mr. Speaker, we learned through the postal workers' own paper-with a circulation of 60,000 copies- that a rather expensive advertising campaign had been launched to explain the new home delivery system through community boxes.
Indeed here is the question I put to the Minister: How can he allow Canada Post to devote so much energy and so many human and material resources to sell Canadians on a postal rate increase they do not want and a delivery system which they never did and never will accept? If they were to accept this, if the community box delivery system were to become the Government's permanent policy as of tomorrow, we would be creating second class citizens. In other words, people go to the trouble of investing and buying new houses which spur the construction industry and create jobs, yet these people will be penalized, Mr. Speaker, because they will not be getting home delivery like all other Canadians do. I think that it is a social injustice that this Government is creating.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to Recommendation No. 8 of the Marchment Report which stated, and I quote:
Communities in urban areas which do not enjoy daily door-to-door delivery be consulted with a view to offering the choice between alternate day letter carrier service or daily mail service through the use of group, community or post office boxes.
There was no proper consultation, Mr. Speaker. Also, the same report had recommended that another five years be granted to Canada Post to get rid of its deficit. Here is what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced on February 26, 1986, and I should like to quote from page 8 of his Budget's speech:
The Marchment Committee has recommended another five years to reach the break-even point. This is not acceptable.
Following discussions with the President of Canada Post, the Government has requested a new operating plan to improve productivity at Canada Post so that the Corporation will reduce its operating deficit to zero by the end of fiscal 1987-
Adjournment Debate
88. The Government is confident that by taking further steps to improve productivity and efficiency, Canada Post and its workers can meet the objctive of self-sufficiency while improving reliability of service to the people of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the Government has obviously decided to go completely against these two recommendations of the Marchment Commission, and we know that Canada Post wants now to increase by 2 cents the cost of stamps for first class mail.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to use the short time remaining at my disposal to mention also that this is the second increase in the cost of stamps since the Progressive Conservative Party came to power. As a matter of fact, when the former Minister responsible for Canada Post announced on June 20, 1985, that the Government was giving the green light to Post Canada to increase by 2 cents the cost of stamps, he said, and I quote in English, Mr. Speaker:
Mr. Beatty said that, before future rate increases are considered by the federal government, Cabinet will expect Canada Post to implement new measures to improve productivity.
Canadians do not believe that any new measures have been implemented to improve productivity. The only thing which was implemented was community boxes. People in new homes in Canada are not receiving home delivery. Therefore, the Government and the Canada Post Corporation is discriminating against Canadians and creating second-class citizens. Perhaps tomorrow Canadians will learn the truth. All Canadians await the so-called postal business plan which the Government is supposed to announce to indicate how we will receive our mail in the future. We hope that tomorrow we will still have only one class of citizen in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. M. Forrestall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
subtopic: CANADA POST-PLAN TO PROMOTE POSTAL RATE INCREASES- UTILIZATION OF HUMAN AND MATERIAL RESOURCES- REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my judgment in the past two years Canada Post has shown a remarkable capacity and ability to do more with less. As the Hon. Member indicated, tomorrow at three o'clock in this Chamber the Minister will be tabling the corporate plan for Canada Post. We do not have to wait for the future to identify the progress already being made and that which has been made in the last couple of years.
Over the past two years the volume of mail handled by the Corporation has increased by almost 7 per cent. At the same time the number of employees has been reduced by 2,000, a saving of some $60 million. Not only has the volume of mail increased, but Canada Post is serving more and more homes and businesses. Service has been extended to over 200,000 new homes and businesses since September of 1984.
The Minister will be reporting on strides being made in improving the reliability of service. These have been made by the introduction of new and consistent standards, systems and procedures into the Corporation's operations in order to keep the mail flowing smoothly and to handle any potential problems as they start to develop.
1086

November 4, 1986
Adjournment Debate
At the same time as these improvements have been implemented, Canada Post has gone through a period of downsizing. One thousand vacant positions have not been filled in the past two years. As I just indicated, in the same period,
2,000	employees have left the Corporation through normal and accelerated attrition. I might add that this has not been at the expense of those employees actively involved in moving the mail. The administrative and management group which has been criticized as being top heavy has been reduced by 10 per cent. Senior management, in fact, has been reduced by some 26 per cent.
Non-salary expenses have also been remarkably contained. Through strict control, these expenses have only been raised by $5 million. I note that inflation alone would have added $50 million in itself.
Canada Post is a business, of course, and like all businesses the heart of its financial structure is in revenue. In the same two-year period we have been discussing, Canada Post increased its revenue by some 15 per cent. Although the Corporation did raise its rates in June of last year, 60 per cent of this increase in revenue is directly linked to sales growth and other factors.
I do not mean to bombard my hon. colleagues with figures, I simply want to point out that there is much evidence that Canada Post Corporation has begun its much needed turnaround.
The past few years should give us confidence that breaking even can be achieved and should give us reason to look forward to the corporate plan when it is introduced tomorrow.
Perhaps I can suggest that we applaud the Post Office instead of bashing it.

subtopic: ABORTION-COLLECTION OF STATISTICS
ABORTION-COLLECTION OF STATISTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in August of this year Statistics Canada announced in a letter to health care administrators that it will no longer compile statistics on therapeutic abortions in Canada. The decision was taken to cease funding for the collection and analysis of abortion statistics as part of an over-all expenditure reduction. Statistics Canada is now processing 1985 abortion data, however it has stated that 1986 data already gathered will not be processed.
When I questioned the Minister responsible for Statistics Canada last week, I was told that meetings were being held between Statistics Canada and officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare, and that the Minister was awaiting a report from this group. There were indications at that time from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) that his Department could compile statistics on abortion from medicare payments to doctors.
It is incredible that it is not a priority of our national statistical record-keeping agency to keep statistics on abortion which is the most controversial social issue facing Canadians
today. Surely an agency that can tell us how many bathrooms there are in this country should be able to tell us how many unborn Canadians are killed by abortion each year.
The suggestion that the Department of Health and Welfare gather abortion data from provincial medicare payments simply will not work. In 1977, the committee on the operation of the abortion law, under Chairman Robin Badgley, stated that:
Provincial medicare insurance commissions maintain information on the procedures paid for under existing fee payment schedules for physicians. Because there are sizeable variations between the provinces in how procedures are classified for payment, and in particular, how these relate to induced abortion, no uniform summary from these sources can be made for the country.
I submit that in order to properly compile and analyse the data needed to provide the level of information now published under the therapeutic abortion program, the Department of National Health and Welfare would in fact need to duplicate the services and expertise now available from Statistics Canada, with the result being no cost saving to the taxpayers of Canada at all.
We need to know more, not less, about abortion if we are to resolve this social dilemma. We need to tell Canadians that one in five women seeking abortion is in fact seeking a second or third abortion. We need to tell Canadians that nearly 200 babies killed each year in Canadian hospitals are over 20 weeks of gestation. In order to absorb the ghastly statistics, we need to realize that 10 times the number of Canadians have been killed in the womb than in war. We need to wonder why one out of every four children conceived in the Province of British Columbia is aborted.	-
The information published each year by StatsCan has provided us with gruesome but necessary information on the practice of abortion in this country. We are able to assess the ages of the women involved, whether they are married or single, the age at which they abort their children, trends in urban and rural areas and provincial differences in the rate of abortion. All of this information helps those who address this problem in terms of supporting and caring for women seeking abortion. Alternatives to abortions will be much harder to establish if we cannot give an accurate profile of those who seek it in the first place.
One of the reasons given by Statistics Canada for the cutting of the therapeutic abortion data is that the data collected does not reflect the true numbers of abortions performed in Canada. StatsCan has collected data on legal abortions and not on the thousands of illegal abortions taking place in free standing clinics, mainly in the Province of Quebec.
In other words, the number of illegal abortions has risen to the extent that information on abortions performed in hospitals no longer gives valid data with which to assess the problem. Surely the solution to this dilemma cannot be to stop gathering the data because it is not the statistics themselves which are
November 4, 1986

the problem, but the illegal abortions being performed contrary to the duly enacted Criminal Code of this country. The federal Government must make it known to the provinces, Quebec and Ontario in particular, that Section 251 of the Criminal Code must be enforced.
Each year nearly 65,000 unborn Canadians are killed in Canadian hospitals. Sheer numbers alone indicate the magnitude of the problem. But we need more than total numbers. We need all the information we can get on abortion, statistical and otherwise, if we are ever to solve this problem. The gathering of therapeutic abortion data by Statistics Canada must be re-established immediately to help all Canadians resolve the issue of abortion in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of Supply and Services):
subtopic: ABORTION-COLLECTION OF STATISTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I share the opinion of the Toronto Member for Willowdale (Mr. Oostrom) that we must have objective and reliable data on abortions in Canada. The issues related to the debate on abortion are complex and if the statistical data can help us to gain a better understanding of them, I think that it is important for us to have these data.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, since I have been the Minister responsible for Statistics Canada, I have been able to see for myself to what extent this agency plays an essential role by providing data on all major issues facing Canadian society. Few subjects are debated in this House without our relying on data from Statistics Canada.
Having said this, Mr. Speaker, like all federal agencies, Statistics Canada always tries to improve its programs and is completely supportive of the efforts made by our Government to control its expenditures.
In this context, last spring, my predecessor undertook, in close cooperation with the chief statistician, a review of all departmental programs to establish our priorities.
Good statistics on abortion would certainly have been viewed as a priority, but the program then in existence was judged less important because the data compiled dealt only
Adjournment Debate
with therapeutic abortions authorized under Section 18 of the Criminal Code 1969 Amendment Act. Since the data was incomplete, our investigation had only limited usefulness and could even be misleading in certain cases.
Mr. Speaker, as a woman and a minister in a government concerned with social issues, I recognize the needs expressed by many people who wish to obtain statistical data on abortion. Consequently, my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), and myself have asked the officials of our Departments to examine all possible solutions which would enable Statistics Canada to continue to provide relevant information on this issue.
I am happy to announce today that the publication of data on abortion will be maintained. A new method for compiling the data will however be used. Our yearly estimates will from now on be based on data from the provincial records of doctors' fees. These estimates will be more complete than the present data since they will include abortions practiced in Quebec clinics.
On the other hand, they will be less detailed because these records contain little information on socio-demographic and medical factors. However, Statistics Canada officials have identified a means to counter this problem. Their review of the information on socio-demographic characteristics previously compiled has shown that changes are relatively slow to occur. It was therefore decided that this information would be published every three years rather than annually.
To implement this program, we shall need the cooperation of hospitals and other provincials organizations. I expect that the provinces will accept to cooperate with us in this most important matter.
